Breaking: How Unlimited Free Stuff from Amazon Almost Ruined My Retirement

📅 07 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2037 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Congratulations!
  • I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon. I was happy with this fun fresh way to beat the winter and wanted to share it with others, so I gave it five stars. But soon after I clicked “Submit”, I got an email from Amazon which remarked something like,.

Recent findings suggest that “Congratulations! You’ve been selected to join Amazon Vine for writing helpful reviews!”.

I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.

“Hey, that’s cool”, I thought, “Who doesn’t like free stuff?

Especially since I’ve already been writing product reviews out of the goodness of my heart – why not be rewarded for it?”.

So without giving it much further thought, I clicked “accept” on their terms and conditions and joined the program.

And so began a saga that has taken me on a surprising journey over the past nine months causing me to:.

Okay, I’ll admit that there were also some upsides. My original idea was partly to save some money, by getting stuff I genuinely would have bought anyway, in a way that sounded fun. And that did happen – I saved at least a few thousand dollars on tools and materials for my construction business and the MMM-HQ Coworking space, for free. Plus, at least some of the motivation for signing up was to put myself through an experiment so I could write this blog article about it. And if you’re reading this, it looks like that happened too.

But I was still surprised at how powerful the combination of small nudges and incentives from Amazon was able to hijack my frugality instincts –  and get me to do a bunch of work that wasn’t really the best use of my time.

In a recent development, so I figured if we review my journey and break it down with a bit of Behavioral Science, we could all learn a few valuable things by laughing at Mr. Money Mustache’s folly.

Scarcity Brain and the Online Casino Effect.

One of the most interesting books I’ve read in recent years is Michael Easter’s Scarcity Brain. It’s an exploration of the sneaky ways that modern gambling platforms, marketing and social media algorithms are all built upon two weaknesses in our evolutionary programming:.

As I look back now, I realize that I fell straight into those same traps, because the Vine program has all the key properties of a casino or a TikTok feed:.

Sources indicate that but occasionally, there will be genuinely useful things like super nice light fixtures, tools and plumbing parts, an EV charger, and even some clothing. My favorite ridiculous Eagle shirt as featured in the Mustachianism music video was an Amazon Vine find.

As were a whole supply of super-realistic artificial plants, which while tacky in principle, have been amazing for hard-to-water courtyard garden areas at the MMM HQ.

I also had a lot of fun roping in friends and coworkers from HQ to help and share in the bounty. I let them help me request and review stuff that they wanted, and then they got to keep it. This seemed like a win/win because we shared the work and the fun of laughing at some of the ridiculous products available.

Still, as I went through this experiment this spring and summer and allowed the system to coax me into doing 80 reviews so I could upgrade my account from Vine Silver to Vine Gold*, I noticed something didn’t feel quite right.

I was checking the Vine page every day for scores, even when I didn’t actually need anything. It would usually be a bust, but just often enough, something I actually wanted would come up, and I’d order it before it was too late. Scarcity and unpredictable rewards at work.

Then the bounty would come, I’d unpack it and photograph it with assembly-line speed so I could batch-write all the reviews once per week or so. For every review I did, I was spending time I’d rather spend doing something else. And for every questionable item I got, I was creating pollution and trash from its manufacturing and packaging – directly contradicting the main values of my life and my reason for writing this blog. And I saw all of this, yet I kept doing it!

So Was This The Downfall of MMM?

According to recent reports, during the worst of this consumerism bender, things were dire. I was getting packages almost every day and my recycling bin was overflowing with cardboard. My son and my girlfriend started laughing at some of my more frivolous purchases, so I found myself discreetly tucking away the boxes when they were around to evade scrutiny.

But eventually, I moved into a recovery stage. I had been letting this habit continue out of laziness and as a form of procrastination: it’s very easy to order shit online and pretend I’m doing something useful, and much more difficult to get moving to do the things that really make my life enjoyable.

But I’m old enough to know that hitting the running trails and the gym for my daily workouts, and making progress on all my construction projects, and focusing on the computer as a creative tool rather than an entertainment device so I can get stuff done like this blog post, are the things that bring me the most joy.

Admittedly, some of the sucky factors of the Vine program helped make it easier to recover too. For every genuinely useful thing I found like a contractor-grade extension cord, I had to scan through endless screens of trinkets which not only wasted my time but actually pissed me off at their very existence.

It has been revealed that I also noticed some of the deliberately reviewer-unfriendly features built into the program which reminded me that we reviewers are definitely just low-wage workers rather than any form of VIP. The search functionality is crap, and there is no way to filter or sort the results, because they want you to have to look through everything and they don’t care about the value of your time.

Sources indicate that then there is the hilariously bureaucratic AI-based evaluation system which would occasionally flag my totally tame, factual reviews as “Not meeting our Community Standards” without explaining what the problem was. So I’d have to go in and edit my review, randomly changing a couple of words and maybe some punctuation, and suddenly the AI would be pacified and accept my review. Just dumb.

This is What “Fuck You Money” is For!

It dawned on me that for many people, this is just what “work” looks like. You are given a bunch of tasks and a bunch of rules to follow, in a system you didn’t create and don’t get much say in changing. And then as long as you crank out your TPS Reports without rocking the boat too much, you get your paycheck.

It reminded me of the Uber Driving experiment I did way back in 2017: as soon as I started working as a driver, I could immediately see dozens of improvements that could be made to the system that would make it function better for both drivers and passengers. But since I wasn’t the boss, nobody wanted to hear my ideas.

According to recent reports, experiences like these remind me that while I love hard work and I love learning latest things every day, I greatly prefer being the boss. And I’ve gotten pretty damned accustomed to it after 20 years of financial independence, so I see no need to give it up.

One interesting “gotcha” of the Vine program is that they do keep track of all the free stuff you get and send you a 1099 for its retail value at the end of the year. So it’s not really free, just discounted to whatever your marginal tax rate is (about 25% for me this year). If we peek into my account right now, this is how my 2025 is looking:.

Sources indicate that so I got about $7000 worth of stuff, and could owe up to $1750 of tax on it. In my case, about 75% of it was “sold” to my business for commercial use (construction supplies which I used on jobs or HQ renovations) so it was effectively converted into real income rather than just tax burden. Some of it was stuff I would have bought anyway for my own house which I’ll gladly pay the taxes on. But there is also probably about $1000 of pure nonsense in there as well, for which I’ll owe a tax bill of $250 as penance for my itchy trigger finger on that “Order” button.

According to recent reports, thanks to some advice from wise readers in the comments (below), I have since learned that in most cases you can mark down this estimated value by 80% before declaring it – because you have effectively eliminated most of the resale value by opening and reviewing the product. Thus my tax bill will be more like $50 rather than $250. More detail in this Reddit discussion here.

In a recent development, so here we are today. While I admit that I didn’t explicitly cancel my account, I used the “Keystone Habit” trick to override the temptation to view the Vine page – mapping that browser bookmark to my daily habits list instead, a little chart which I call my “Badassity Tracker”. The net result is that every time I click it, I’m taken straight to a reminder to get up from the computer and do a quick round of exercise, so I do that instead.

And of course my writing of this article may be a violation of the terms and conditions of the program (“the first rule of Vine is to not talk about Vine”), so it might even get canceled on me. (and if so I’ll let you know because that would be funny story as well).

Industry observers note that but I learned a lot about habits and addiction, and realized that this same feeling might be what drives people into One More Year Syndrome, as they keep working even when they can afford to quit. I have now coached enough people through this situation to see it is way more common than I would have ever guessed.

Recent findings suggest that as with all MMM articles, there’s a real life lesson in this story. It’s not really about Vine or me or my habits, it’s about you continuing to look at yourself and your life, and always questioning your own assumptions or patterns. And asking the people you trust most for feedback as well:.

According to recent reports, we will never be perfect, but the great news is we don’t have to be. All it takes is a little bit of self reflection and putting ourselves on a slightly better path, as often as we can as life goes on. We are all on a very long journey, so even a tiny course correction can make a huge difference in where we end up.

Industry News: Teacher Loan Forgiveness Cancels Up to $17,500 – but Costs 5 Years of PSLF Credit

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (420 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, teach full time for five school years in a row at a low-income school, and Teacher Loan Forgiveness can cancel up to $17,500 of your subsidized and unsubsidized federal loans, depending on your subject.
  • The comparison starts with your subject, which sets the cap on Teacher Loan Forgiveness (TLF).
  • Sources indicate that the catch is what TLF does to Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, teach full time for five school years in a row at a low-income school, and Teacher Loan Forgiveness can cancel up to $17,500 of your subsidized and unsubsidized federal loans, depending on your subject. But those years can’t also count toward Public Service Loan Forgiveness, which has no cap, so compare the two before you apply.

The comparison starts with your subject, which sets the cap on Teacher Loan Forgiveness (TLF). Secondary math and science teachers and elementary or secondary special education teachers can get up to $17,500, and other teachers up to $5,000.

Sources indicate that the catch is what TLF does to Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF). PSLF cancels whatever federal Direct Loan balance remains after 120 qualifying monthly payments, made over at least 10 years at a public school or another qualifying employer. Take TLF, and your payments from those five years stop counting toward PSLF, so you’d need 120 more.

For a small balance, TLF beats waiting for PSLF. A high school math teacher who borrowed $16,000 can have what’s left canceled after year five, since it’s under her cap. A colleague who also teaches math intends to stay in public schools and repay on an income-driven proposal, which sets payments by income. With $60,000 in loans, she’d get at most $17,500 from TLF and likely far more from PSLF at year 10, so she skips TLF.

Before you count on TLF, confirm three things:.

According to recent reports, with a balance under your cap, you can ask your loan servicer each year for a TLF forbearance, which pauses payments so you don’t pay down debt TLF would cancel. Interest still builds and can push your balance past the cap.

After year five, have your principal, superintendent, or HR office certify the Teacher Loan Forgiveness Application, then send it to your servicer, one form per servicer.

Before you choose, use StudentAid.gov’s Repayment Calculator to compare what you’d pay in total under each program, since TLF can’t be undone after it’s granted.

Borrowing From Family to Start a Business? Sign a Note First

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (505 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that before family lends you startup money, put the terms in a note you both sign: the amount, interest rate, payment schedule, and who repays it if the business closes.
  • A handshake leaves each of you free to remember a different deal, and the difference shows up the first time a payment is late.
  • It has been revealed that start by agreeing that it’s a loan, repaid on a schedule.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that before family lends you startup money, put the terms in a note you both sign: the amount, interest rate, payment schedule, and who repays it if the business closes. Set the rate at or above the applicable federal rate, a minimum the IRS publishes monthly, so no part of the loan counts as a gift.

A handshake leaves each of you free to remember a different deal, and the difference shows up the first time a payment is late.

It has been revealed that start by agreeing that it’s a loan, repaid on a schedule. Money your parents don’t want back is a gift, and a parent who gives you more than the annual gift tax exclusion in one year files a gift tax return. If they want a share of the profits, it’s a stake, which makes them part owners who get nothing back if the business fails.

According to recent reports, if the loan charges less than the applicable federal rate (AFR), the IRS’s below-market loan rules can treat the interest your parents gave up as a gift from them. In some cases, the IRS also counts it as income they owe tax on.

In the note, formally a promissory note, two terms need the most thought. The first is whether you or your business owes it. Money lent to your limited liability company (LLC) is generally its debt, not yours, so your parents carry the risk if it closes. The second is what happens to the balance if the business closes, whether you keep paying from your own income, pause the payments, or your parents forgive the rest.

In a recent development, say a son borrows $20,000 from his parents for four years. The IRS’s mid-term rate applies to loans over three years and up to nine. Suppose that rate is just under 5% when he gets the money, so they charge 5%. Forty-eight automatic transfers of about $461 repay it with about $2,100 in interest, and no one has to bring up a payment at a holiday dinner.

Industry observers note that ask for no more than your parents could afford to give away, since a new business can close before it repays anyone. Then give them a few days to decide how to lend without losing money or the relationship.

Look up the AFR for the month you get the money, write a rate at least that high into the note, and set up the automatic transfer the day it arrives.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that pay for startup equipment and inventory with a business credit card that charges 0% interest on purchases for a year or more.
  • It has been revealed that borrowing at 0% costs less than most startup loans.
  • Industry observers note that the catch is that the debt is yours.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that pay for startup equipment and inventory with a business credit card that charges 0% interest on purchases for a year or more. Divide the balance by the number of months the 0% rate lasts, round up, and set that payment on autopay, so your card is paid off before its regular rate starts.

It has been revealed that borrowing at 0% costs less than most startup loans. A microloan through the U.S. Small Business Administration, for one, generally charges 8% to 13% interest, depending on the lender.

Industry observers note that the catch is that the debt is yours. Small-business cards typically carry a personal guarantee, so you and the business both owe the balance, a Federal Reserve report to Congress found. When the business has little or no credit history, the issuer relies more on your personal credit.

According to recent reports, the same report explains that the protections in the CARD Act, the 2009 federal law on credit card practices, apply to personal cards, not business cards. So your card’s own terms decide what a late payment costs. On U.S. Bank’s Business Shield, one late payment, or one that bounces, ends the 0% rate early.

Charge only purchases that will bring in money soon, like the equipment you’ll work with and inventory you’ll sell. Months of rent and other bills are a poor fit, since a slow launch may not earn enough to repay them before the 0% rate ends.

According to recent reports, the longer the 0% period, the smaller each monthly payment can be. Bank of America’s Platinum Plus business card gives 0% for 15 billing cycles on purchases when you apply online, then a variable rate of 14.99% to 25.99%. The 0% period starts when the account opens, so apply when you’re ready to buy.

It has been revealed that then divide the balance by the number of months the 0% rate lasts, round up, and set that amount on autopay, the same proposal that pays off a balance transfer in time. A photographer who charges $8,400 in cameras and lenses to a card with 0% for 15 months would pay $560 a month by that math. Rounding up to $600 clears it in 14 months, with a month to spare.

Set up that autopay the day the card arrives, so no payment comes in late while you’re busy launching.

From the best small-business credit cards, pick one whose 0% period is long enough for a payment your business can afford.

Startup Accelerators Cost You a Stake – Apply Only if You’ll Raise From Investors

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (490 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apply to a startup accelerator only if your business could grow fast enough to raise money from investors.
  • According to recent reports, at the best-known programs, the seed money is no grant.
  • Y Combinator’s standard deal puts $500,000 into each startup it accepts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apply to a startup accelerator only if your business could grow fast enough to raise money from investors. In exchange for a slice of your company, it usually gives you seed money, mentors, and introductions to investors. If you’ll never sell a stake, get free advice from SCORE or a Small Business Development Center instead.

According to recent reports, at the best-known programs, the seed money is no grant. Every dollar of it buys a piece of your manufacturer.

Y Combinator’s standard deal puts $500,000 into each startup it accepts. Of that, $125,000 buys a fixed 7% of your organization, and Y Combinator invests the other $375,000 through a SAFE, a contract that turns into shares when investors later buy your stock at a set price. Techstars takes a fixed 5% for $20,000 and, in most programs, puts another $200,000 into the same kind of SAFE. Either way, the program’s stake grows past its fixed 7% or 5% once its SAFE turns into shares.

Along with the cash, that stake gets you mentors and introductions to investors. Many programs end with a demo day, where you pitch your company to investors. That trade is worth making only if you’ll go on to raise money from angel investors or venture capital firms. A two-founder software startup that gives up a fixed 7%, then raises its first round from investors it met at demo day, gets what it paid for.

According to recent reports, A business that won’t raise from investors should look for help that costs no stake. Universities, cities, and companies run incubators that can offer workspace and advice. Some are free, while others charge a fee or take a stake, so ask first. A bakery that rents low-cost kitchen space from a city incubator and gets coaching there keeps the whole business. SCORE’s mentors advise U.S. business owners for free, and Small Business Development Centers offer no-cost consulting.

For a startup that will raise money, judge a program by its people and its terms. Find out which investors come to its demo day and whether its mentors have built companies like yours. Read the terms of both the fixed stake and the SAFE, and check whether you must move, since Y Combinator’s three-month program meets in person in San Francisco.

Before you apply, ask each program what share of the companies in its last two classes raised money within a year of demo day.

The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In many states, public colleges waive tuition for residents once they reach 60, 62, or 65, so you can take regular college classes for little more than books and fees. Ask a nearby public college’s registrar for its tuition waiver for older students, and find out when waiver students may register.

The other rules vary by state. Florida law lets the state’s public universities and colleges waive tuition and fees for residents 60 and older who audit classes, meaning they sit in without earning credit. At the University of North Georgia, Georgia residents 62 and older can take classes for credit or audit them, but they can’t register for fall or spring terms until the first day of classes. Kentucky law requires the state’s public colleges to waive all tuition and fees for residents 65 and older unless classes are full.

Under North Georgia’s waiver, a 66-year-old Georgia resident taking two history classes a semester pays for her books, supplies, and any lab fees, but no tuition.

It has been revealed that to find your state’s version, call the registrar or continuing education office at a nearby public college and ask for its tuition waiver for older students. Bring proof of age and residency, such as a driver’s license, and ask whether you can earn credit and which fees you still owe. Where no nearby school offers one, ask your state’s higher education agency which campuses do.

Recent findings suggest that if no seat opens, look up the nearest Osher Lifelong Learning Institute. The institutes, at colleges in all 50 states, run noncredit classes for people 50 and older, with no tests or grades, for fees that vary by institute. A community college’s continuing education classes and universities’ free online courses are other options.

For a waiver seat, call the registrar a semester ahead, since you may need to apply for admission by the college’s usual deadline before the waiver covers a class.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that to make money teaching English online, apply where your background fits.
  • Sources indicate that neither kind requires a degree or a teaching certificate.
  • Recent findings suggest that without a certificate, start with Cambly, a conversation app that pays $0.17 for each minute you’re in a lesson, or $10.20 for a full hour.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that to make money teaching English online, apply where your background fits. Without a teaching certificate, start on a conversation app, which pays a flat rate. With one, use a lesson marketplace, where you set your own price and the certificate justifies charging more. Then make yourself available when students book most.

Sources indicate that neither kind requires a degree or a teaching certificate. Credentials change how much you can earn.

Recent findings suggest that without a certificate, start with Cambly, a conversation app that pays $0.17 for each minute you’re in a lesson, or $10.20 for a full hour. An hour with gaps between calls pays less than $10.20, and Cambly is temporarily limiting how many upcoming tutors it takes.

With a certificate, set your own price on Preply, a lesson marketplace where English tutors charge $15 to $25 an hour on average. Preply keeps the whole fee for each fresh student’s trial lesson and, while you’re new, 33% of every lesson after that, a cut that falls to 18% as your teaching hours add up. At $15 an hour, you’d keep $10.05, a bit less than Cambly’s $10.20 for the same hour. A TEFL (Teaching English as a Foreign Language) certificate can let you charge more, Preply’s own guide to becoming a tutor states, and at $25 you’d keep $16.75 after the same cut.

Count the costs, too. You need a quiet room, a headset with a microphone, and a reliable internet connection. Both platforms treat you as an independent contractor, so once your net earnings reach $400 in a year, you owe the IRS a 15.3% self-employment tax for Social Security and Medicare, on top of income tax. Set aside part of every payout for both in a separate savings account.

Set your hours around demand, not just your free time. Preply’s calendar shades the times students in your subject are most likely to book, and Cambly’s Priority Hours send you calls from new students during hours you claim. A parent who teaches from 6 to 8 a.m. Eastern can finish before the kids wake up, while it’s evening for learners in Japan and South Korea.

In a recent development, keep those hours the same every week. Cambly says a consistent schedule helps attract regular students, and Preply says students are more likely to stay with a tutor who’s always free at the same time.

Become a Virtual Assistant – Sell One Service You Already Do Well

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that start as a virtual assistant by selling one service you’ve done in a past job, such as managing an inbox and calendar or keeping the books, instead of offering help with anything.
  • Business owners hire a virtual assistant to hand off a specific task.
  • Your past jobs tell you which service to sell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that start as a virtual assistant by selling one service you’ve done in a past job, such as managing an inbox and calendar or keeping the books, instead of offering help with anything. Price it by the hour or as a flat monthly package, and pitch it first to people who already know your work.

Business owners hire a virtual assistant to hand off a specific task. An offer that names the task and its price is easy to accept, while “I can help with anything” leaves the owner to work out both.

Your past jobs tell you which service to sell. A former executive assistant can manage an owner’s inbox and calendar, an office manager can keep a small manufacturer’s books, and someone from a call center can answer customer emails and chats.

Industry observers note that base your price on what employers pay for the same work. In May 2025, the Bureau of Labor Statistics put the median employee wage at $21.53 an hour for customer service representatives, $23.23 for secretaries and administrative assistants, and $24.36 for bookkeeping, accounting, and auditing clerks. Set your rate above the figure for your kind of work. As a contractor, you pay self-employment tax, both the employer’s and the employee’s share of Social Security and Medicare, and nobody pays you for sick days or hours spent finding clients.

Sources indicate that charge by the hour for work that comes and goes. For weekly tasks, sell a flat monthly package that spells out what it covers. Say a former office manager keeps the books for three local contractors, about two hours a week each, for a flat $350 a month per client. That’s about $40 an hour and $1,050 a month.

In a recent development, pitch former bosses, coworkers, and clients first, since they’ve seen your work. Then look for clients through local business groups, like your chamber of commerce, and freelance marketplaces. Put each client on a short contract that lists the tasks, the rate, when you’re paid, and how either side can end it.

The Federal Trade Commission warns about fake virtual assistant jobs that pay with a check. The fake employer asks you to deposit it, keep part as your pay, and forward the rest to another person. Then the check bounces, and your bank wants the full amount back. A real client never asks you to forward part of a payment.

#56615. My Unexpected Journey to Hormone Replacement (TRT)

My Unexpected Journey to Hormone Replacement (TRT)

📅 16 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2722 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a man of Science, I’m supposed to hide my enthusiasm about this somewhat controversial subject, and instead direct you only to the peer-reviewed studies.
  • According to recent reports, but man, I feel like I’ve stumbled upon the fountain of youth here.
  • I’ve been interested in optimization and trying to get the most out of my body and mind since I was a little kid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a man of Science, I’m supposed to hide my enthusiasm about this somewhat controversial subject, and instead direct you only to the peer-reviewed studies.

According to recent reports, but man, I feel like I’ve stumbled upon the fountain of youth here. And the more I dig into the details and the hype and controversy surrounding the field of Hormone Replacement therapy, the more I need to share the word about it to my fellow middle-aged people (both men and women).

I’ve been interested in optimization and trying to get the most out of my body and mind since I was a little kid. I started vacuuming up all the training and nutrition books and magazines I could find while I was just a teenager, and that field still remains a favorite of mine over 30 years later. And if you’re a long-time reader here you’ve been reminded plenty of times of this interest, because health has always been the very heart of Mustachianism.

But a funny thing has been happening in the last ten years: even as I kept honing the healthy living habits and trying my best to improve, there seemed to be a force pulling me back almost as hard. So despite working a bit harder and smarter every year, I still felt myself riding a gradually declining tide of energy, motivation, and physical stamina.

“Perhaps this is just what it means to grow old”, I thought to myself,.

“But I’m still gonna keep fighting it!”.

Yet there was one thing that didn’t quite fit. Why was I having this decline in energy, when some of my older friends weren’t? And why was I still seeing people out there in their 50s, 60s and well beyond doing things that I felt too tired to do today?

According to recent reports, one of these tireless friends is a guy named Kevin, who is the personification of the highly energetic successful middle-aged man. He’s a semi-retired serial entrepreneur (and extreme rock climber) who lives in Boulder. And through an interesting twist of fate, in April of 2025 he invited me out for a hike right around the time I was doing all this wondering. And during this hike (and climb) he told me about his latest venture, a boutique men’s health company that specializes in helping men just like us get their youth back through the process of testosterone replacement therapy.

Long story short: his ideas planted a seed in my head, which led to a bunch of research and a growing interest in trying TRT myself. I had of course heard about the process, but for some reason never considered doing it until I heard Kevin’s enthusiasm: he had been on it for several years, and according to him it is a “night and day difference” in all the things you want in life: energy, focus, thinking speed, and of course physical health.

According to recent reports, another convenient twist of fate is that I happen to be dating an REI doctor – a Reproductive Endocrinologist and Infertility specialist who has two board certifications in exactly the relevant bodily systems that are affected by these hormones. And while she was initially skeptical that I needed more Testosterone (and in her practice she regularly sees the downsides of men taking the stuff too early in life and thus compromising their own fertility), she has followed along and helped me learn at each step of this process, eventually becoming fully in support of the program.

So I signed up as a test customer for Kevin’s newly introduced manufacturer, which is called Bolt Health. I worked with their doctor to get a baseline blood test and review my numbers compared to all the past tests I’ve collected, and as it turned out, my levels had been dropping consistently over the years, and the latest test was by far the lowest ever.

Even more telling, my age-related drop in Testosterone was correlating perfectly with my decline in energy and motivation:.

It has been revealed that the next step was a prescription for a tiny daily dose of supplemental T, which arrived at my house the next week along with instructions for how to use it. And so began the journey.

Now let’s jump forward seven months to the present day as I write this.

And wow, what a great year it has been! I only wish I had known and tried this a few years earlier, because I’m getting a lot more out of my life.

It’s not a night-and-day difference for me, but more like a 50% boost in overall youthfulness and energy. The biggest subjective change is that I just don’t have sucky tired days anymore, which was the main problem with my life before: wasting too much of my precious freedom due to not having the energy to enjoy it.

It has been revealed that this is why I’ve become somewhat of an evangelist for hormone replacement therapy for people from about age 45 onwards. It won’t work for everyone – if your levels are already pretty high, you don’t get the same boost. Two of my male friends tried TRT and quit because they didn’t notice any benefit. But these same two guys already had plenty of energy to begin with, which is usually a sign that the body has what it needs.

It has been revealed that it turns out I am very late to this party. Although Testosterone supplementation started out as a niche practice in the 1940s, from the 2010s onward it has been everywhere.

TRT is the reason you see every actor suddenly showing up buff overnight for their superhero roles and it’s also why so many of today’s CEOs don’t look anything like yesterday’s CEOs.

It has been revealed that in many cases, it has gone too far with young men using it just to gain muscle for the beach or the football field, and questionable online providers (aka “Prescription Mills”) handing out prescriptions to anyone with a valid credit card – with profit as their sole motive. It became overhyped in certain pockets of Bro Culture, where every Bro eventually receives the advice “Bro! You need to get on the T!” from another Bro, and therefore does it. And some of this reputation surely contributed to my own skepticism.

Sources indicate that but there’s a lot of valid science behind TRT, if you’re the right candidate and you take the right dosage. And because of that, I feel it is probably under-hyped in my own demographic, the Nerdy Tech Worker Semi Retired Dad contingent. And that’s why I’m writing this blog post, because there are a lot of us out there.

Many of us just tend to work with what we were given, and accept that aging means slowing down. And for those of us already enjoying an early retirement, we have the option of unlimited rest and recuperation time, so who really cares if we get tired a bit more often? After all, what better way to flex one’s wealth than with a decadent Tuesday Afternoon Nap while everyone else is stuck in the office?

While this seemingly healthy attitude has a lot of positive aspects, it can also mask a real problem which may be easily fixable. Because sometimes, the only thing that’s even better than an afternoon nap, is having the energy and motivation to go out for an afternoon hike, bike ride or adventure with friends. More energy is also pretty darned useful if you’re still raising kids or trying to do well in your career as a person over 45.

How it Actually Works (and What Happened to Me).

Distilling all of the fluffy discussion above into the simplest possible answer: TRT means using a tiny needle to inject a few drops of clear liquid just below the surface of your skin. And you do this by yourself at home, ideally once every morning.

Here’s one of the baby needles I use for my daily dose.The typical serving is less than one tenth of a milliliter, which is only a few drops.

And while the term “needle” sounds scary to some, this is very different from the monstrosities they use to draw blood from your veins. This one is so miniature that you don’t need special training to use it, and you usually don’t even feel it.

According to recent reports, so I began doing this to myself on May 1st of this year, while keeping a daily journal of my results along the way. The results seemed to be almost immediate in all the promised areas, but I know how powerful the Placebo Effect can be so I kept my skeptic’s hat on to see what would happen in the long run.

I was seeing increased energy and motivation as well as lean weight gain through the whole spring and summer, but I remember the first truly shocking observation happened during a mountain vacation in July. I was part of a multi-family trip with lively adults, chaotic kids, early mornings, late nights with a few drinks, very intense high altitude sunshine and nonstop physical activities. It was just the type of situation that would drain my energy pretty quickly in the past.

But on day three I went out on a solo mountain bike ride to explore the area, and as I was climbing a long ascent with the blazing sun cooking me from every angle I just somehow kept having plenty of energy to keep climbing. Then I came down and joined the group for a few games of full-sun pickleball, biked back up the mountain to our cabin, and the story of unlimited energy went on from there.

“Hot Damn”, I thought to myself, “I don’t know whose youthful and tireless body I have inherited here but I’d sure like to keep it!”.

In August, the Bolt Health program scheduled a follow-up blood test for me and sure enough, my Testosterone levels had been boosted from 415 to 730ng/dL, bringing me from the low side of normal to the higher side.

Many labs define “normal” as anywhere between 300 and 1000, which seems strange to me given the huge effect this hormone has on your wellbeing. It’s a bit like saying “Most cars have between 90 and 300 horsepower, so it doesn’t really matter what engine you have”.

I mean yeah, either one will still get you down the road, but which one would you rather be driving?

Since then, it has just been more of the same good results. My improvements ramped up and then just stayed there – so I’m operating at a new, much higher and more enjoyable level of functioning. Energy and motivation are no longer a problem, and I even find myself willing to make longer-term plans again (before this everything beyond same-day planning felt overwhelming). And my body seems to just want to gain strength and size with any excuse. Heavy weights feel lighter and the hard manual labor I still like to spend my time on feels easier for longer. It’s nice to be young again!

So Why Doesn’t Everyone Do This?

According to recent reports, when you dig into the details, hormone replacement is mired in a soup of both real and incorrect information about both its benefits and its risks. And then our well-meaning medical establishment locks this whole container of soup deep in the cabinet with a label that states, “Needs Further Study”. But if you summarize the findings on both sides of the matter, you’ll see this:.

Stuff you should do BEFORE trying TRT:.

The modern American Lifestyle is a Testosterone and Health Crusher. It’s a miracle that anybody feels good ever with the crap that people do to their bodies. So if you’re not already doing all the simple, natural, outdoor things that naturally boost your health, energy, and hormone levels, you’ll want to start with these first. You can find a pretty complete list on my oft-cited Badassity Tracker page.

Since I was already doing all of these things pretty consistently, I felt ready to take the next step and at least consider hormone supplementation. But wait, there’s more!

Many of the problems above are more likely to appear when the body is flooded with too much testosterone. In the bad old days, TRT was administered by sticking a pellet beneath your skin or injecting a large amount into the butt which then gets used up over the next several weeks. One friend recounted a story of extreme moodiness when the pellet was first implanted, ramping down to tiredness by the time the hormone was all gone.

More modern providers like Bolt have fixed this problem by breaking the dose into much smaller servings which you administer each day. The idea is that your levels remain stable, and you need a lot less overall which reduces side effects.

For my part, I have not had any of the negative side effects because I was a pretty ideal candidate in the first place: 50 years old with depressed Testosterone levels but an otherwise healthy lifestyle and no risk factors.

It has been revealed that my hope in sharing this article is to be transparent and hopefully take some of the stigma out of this subject of other people who might benefit. Because in our modern over-connected world, everybody has an opinion on your life, even when you didn’t ask them.

According to recent reports, and it’s not just men – many women in this same age group benefit from Estrogen replacement (and there are even interesting stories about female testosterone supplementation in certain situations as this author shares). The point is that aging is normal, but in some cases there’s a pretty easy way to make it slower.

The great news is that Testosterone itself is a cheap and widely available substance, typically under $50 per month even for people like me without conventional insurance or drug coverage. The expensive part (here in the US) is just the doctor stuff – consultations, blood tests, ongoing analysis and prescription renewals and so on.

The organization that I used is positioned as a premium provider, bundling these services along with a bunch of other men’s health perks and deliveries for a few hundred dollars, which is expensive relative to most other parts of my budget, but still cheap if I consider the life and financial benefits of being 20-50% more energetic and productive.

If you want to be on this program, your final decision will hinge on your income, insurance coverage if applicable, whether your existing doctor can already help you, and how much service and advice you’re willing to pay for.

Industry observers note that note: I decided not to become a Bolt health affiliate because I wanted to write this article without conflict of interest. And I can honestly say, Bolt’s product and service seem great to me because I know and trust the people who run it. But  it’s also the only one I’ve tried. So I don’t know much about the competition and there may be other good options out there. At the very minimum, you can always try one service and switch to another if you don’t like the first one.

In a recent development, I’ve got lots more to say on money and early retirement, and lots of interesting projects in the works now too. So I’m thankful to have stumbled upon this booster for all aspects of life, so I can do more of everything else, for even more decades than I had expected.

I wish this same type of good fortune for you, however you create it.

In the Comments: Do you have questions about hormone replacement or anything else in this article? I’ll try to invite Kevin, Dr. Sean Bender and other knowledgeable people to contribute and answer questions as well.

Breakfast out can easily cost a family of four $40 or more a morning. The government’s per diem, the daily allowance federal employees get on work trips, includes $16 to $23 for breakfast alone, depending on where they travel.

It has been revealed that A hotel that includes breakfast saves you that cost every morning of your stay. Its rate can run higher than a rival’s and still cost your family less, as long as the difference is smaller than what breakfast out would cost.

These 12 chains include breakfast at most or all of their U.S. hotels, grouped here by hotel family.

Marriott Bonvoy’s Platinum Elite status, which takes 50 nights a year to earn by staying, lets members pick points, a breakfast offering, or another gift on arrival, depending on the brand.

In a recent development, some hotel credit cards come with Gold status, no stays required. For a family of four, though, a chain that includes breakfast for everyone in the room does more than a credit that covers two.

Industry observers note that compare each hotel’s total for the night, taxes included, and add what breakfast out would cost your family to the one that doesn’t serve it. Recent findings suggest that the breakfast hotel stops saving you money once the gap between the two rates is bigger than your breakfast bill. Against a $109 room plus that $45 breakfast, the same $159 hotel costs $5 more a night.

Recent findings suggest that before you book, check that the rate you picked includes breakfast and that the serving hours fit your plans. Drury serves breakfast from 6 to 9:30 a.m. on weekdays and 7 to 10 a.m. on weekends, so a family on the road by 6 a.m. would miss it.

On longer stays, a room with a kitchen lets you make lunch and dinner too.

Find what your family spent the last time you ate breakfast out, on a receipt or your card statement, and plug that figure into every hotel comparison on the trip.

For a substantial renovation, price a home equity loan or home equity line of credit (HELOC) first, which usually costs less.

Borrowing against your home equity costs less than a personal loan because the house secures the loan, and that’s also why it’s slower and riskier.

In a recent development, A home equity loan or HELOC usually means an appraisal, closing costs such as title search fees, and a few weeks’ wait for the money. Fall behind on it, and the lender can foreclose. A personal loan usually runs two to seven years, where an equity loan can run 20.

It has been revealed that on a small job, the equity loan’s lower rate doesn’t save much. Say you borrow $15,000 for a bathroom remodel over five years, at 11% on a personal loan with no origination fee or at 8% on a home equity loan with $500 in closing costs. The personal loan’s interest comes to about $4,600 and the equity loan’s to about $3,200, so after its closing costs, the equity loan is only about $800 cheaper. On $50,000 at the same rates and term, the equity loan’s interest runs about $4,400 less than the personal loan’s before closing costs, which makes it worth pricing first for a substantial renovation.

In a recent development, before you apply, get your contractor’s written, fixed-price bid, so the amount you borrow matches a set price, not an estimate. Then rank personal loan offers by annual percentage rate (APR), not interest rate, since the APR includes the origination fee many lenders take out of the loan.

Take the shortest term whose payment fits your budget. At 11%, repaying $15,000 in three years instead of five raises the payment from about $326 to $491 and cuts the interest from about $4,600 to $2,700.

  • But for those of us leaving the workplace in our 30 and 40s, Social Security is just a fuzzy concept in the very distant future.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the world of very early retirement, we tend to ignore one of the most important things for normal retirees: the Social Security program.

Don’t get me wrong, it’s a great thing for the 73 million people who presently draw benefits, and it provides an essential safety net for many who don’t have much income from anywhere else.

But for those of us leaving the workplace in our 30 and 40s, Social Security is just a fuzzy concept in the very distant future. We aren’t thinking about money that eases us into our Golden Years, we need something that starts working now. Plus we’d rather not rely on our government keeping its promises that far into the future.

According to recent reports, those were my thoughts in 2005, when I was just a young retiree myself. But a funny thing happens when time passes: you get older. And you realize that there are plenty of other older people around too. And suddenly, Social Security is an important subject after all, that many people would like to know more about. But there is an endless pile of conflicting opinions:.

But when I did the math on all of this, I realized that it’s more confusing than it needs to be. Because when it comes to deciding on how Social Security fits into your retirement strategy, it really boils down to only one number:.

The Net Present Value of your future lifetime stream of Social Security payments.

That little piece of math jargon might not mean much if you don’t have fond memories of  Economics 101 class. But don’t worry, it’s easy to understand if you think of these two extremes:.

Sources indicate that if you want to retire in your 30s like I did, the value of your future Social Security is pretty close to zero. Even if the government keeps all of its promises, those payments are so far in the future that you need to save a full retirement ‘stash to get through the three decades until it kicks in.

On the other hand, if you’re already over 60 years old, contributed to Social Security throughout your long career and have a low cost of living, you may be eligible for payments that already meet all your needs.

Industry observers note that in this situation, you are set for life. Social Security will in theory cover all your needs and rise automatically with inflation, so you don’t have to save any additional money.

It has been revealed that in between these two extremes, the math gets interesting. Because while most people assume Social Security is useless until you reach full eligibility, the real story is that you can think of it as a chunk of money that you already have right now, which reduces the amount of saving you have to do on your own.

And there’s an easy way to calculate it, with an extremely useful thing called the Net Present Value calculation.

There’s an actual formula for this, but don’t worry you don’t have to memorize it because you can just have any Internet calculator, AI tool or spreadsheet do the math for you.

First let’s calculate the value a young couple might get if they do this calculation at 30 years old. We just have to make a few assumptions to have numbers plug into the formula:.

When you plug in all the numbers and calculate this (the Net Present Value of a 30 year stream of income), the first number you’ll get is $667,166. But that’s not the final answer – that is how much you’d need if you wanted the payments to start right now.

The final step is applying a simpler version of the formula a second time, to account for the fact that you don’t need the money until 32 years from now:.

According to recent reports, at that point, you end up with a number around $98,280. But what does this mean?

It means that if you stuck $98k into an investment account today and let it compound for 32 years, at that point it would be big enough to provide a stream of $4000 payments for the following 30 years. And this even takes future inflation into account!It also means that the 30 year old retirees can mark an imaginary $98k onto their “net worth” spreadsheet and save that much less. Or at least think of it as a nice safety margin.

It has been revealed that if you’re newly introduced to money and math, that may sound like sorcery, but if you’ve been investing for long enough you will understand that it really does work that way. So let’s re-run the example for a couple who is already 62 years old, and needs a $5000 income starting right now, that still needs to last 30 years.

That NPV calculation looks like this:.

And the answer is right around $834,000.

Sources indicate that what this means, is that if they invested $834,000 into a fund that paid out 6% per year for 30 years before running dry, they’d get that exact same $5000 monthly income. And it would keep up with inflation.

Now that we’ve seen these examples from the extreme ends of the spectrum, we can see how this applies in a more typical situation. Here’s one that is loosely based on one from a real person I worked with last year:.

Shane Survivor is 55 and he has been through some hard times. He lost most of his savings in a business blowup a few years back, but really wishes he could still retire soon. His financial picture:.

Most financial advisors would tell him to tough it out and  just keep working until he hits Social Security eligibility. At least 62 to get the minimum benefits, but maybe even longer to get to Full Retirement Age (67) or even until 70 to get the maximum benefit.

But wait! Let’s do the math because who wants to work another fifteen years when you’re already tired of working at 55!

Shane logs into the Social Security website SSA.gov and uses the online tool to calculate what his payout will be. I just did this myself so we can use my numbers:.

Whoa wait a minute, that’s a counterintuitive result! Am I really telling you that it’s actually less valuable to work longer so you can get the higher benefits? The answer is yes, for people who understand the concepts of “investing” and “the time value of money”.

To really understand this, just imagine what would happen if you started taking those payments as early as possible (age 62) and tossed them into an index fund, earning 6% after inflation on average. After the first year, you’d already have about $24,300 and you’d still be piling in that extra two grand per month and the whole snowball would be starting to compound.

By the time your more patient friends started drawing $2796 payments five years later, you’d already have over $137,000. It’s such a major lead that the 67-year-old will never catch up.

And of course, any additional tricks he can apply like streamlining his spending and boosting his income, will make this even faster. I’d give him about three years before reaching liftoff.

So how can YOU use this information to speed up your own retirement?

Recent findings suggest that the net effect of Social Security is that it should help you worry a little less and work a little less. The worrying part should benefit everyone, and the working part is kind of a sliding scale:.

Can we just put this in ONE SIMPLE TABLE based on some reasonable assumptions?

Yes, absolutely! Just to hit the most common situation, let’s assume a household that has.

How much is this future benefit worth you you, based on your current age?

According to recent reports, these aren’t enormous FAT Fire numbers, but every one of them is enough to feel like a meaningful contribution to your eventual early jump into freedom. For example as a 51-year-old, I can look at my number of roughly $350,000 and say yeah, that’s quite a major boost – enough to buy an entire house in many areas of the country or enough to fund multiple lifetimes of high-end groceries. And until now I had never even considered it as part of my retirement savings!

Frequently Asked (or Complained) Questions.

Now that we’ve covered the facts, I can already hear the complaints coming.

What if Social Security is canceled or greatly reduced by the time I reach that age?

Yeah, it might happen, but it’s also a top priority for most voters in our aging population. So it’s hard for politicians to make cuts. What is more likely is that the benefits will be cut for wealthier people. And if you find yourself in that camp (as I do), you won’t actually need the payments.

Industry observers note that sure, it’s not “fair”, but you know what? I can think of more fun ways to enjoy the fact that I’m a rich person rather than complaining about how some government program is “unfair”, and so can you.

Nobody can live on just a Social Security check!

First of all, millions of people do. In fact, last time I checked my own annual spending it was under $30k, most of it on optional luxuries, which is less than my expected payout!

But more importantly, most of us won’t have to, because we are also investing healthy sums on our own.

I’m still scared and worried about something else!

Sources indicate that now this is the root of the matter. In fact, worry is the root of almost all issues. And so that’s what we need to focus on in our future work. For some reason, I have managed to live the last twenty years pretty much completely free from financial worries, and I had assumed everyone else was the same way. But it turns out this is not the case, even among people much wealthier and more advantaged than I am.

So in the next article, we need to get into that.

Log yourself into ssa.gov, and if it’s your first time doing that – congratulations! Note that new people will need to create an account, and they’ll guide you to login.gov for that purpose. Don’t fret, it’s very useful to have this account for multiple reasons.

Bonus Materials: the Quirk of Social Security Contributions.

To illustrate this point, I ran a simulation of two people who each make a $100k salary and contribute accordingly, but one retires after 10 years and that poor second guy works the full 35. Look at the difference in their benefits:.

In a recent development, so the early retiree only worked and contributed about 28% as much as the late retiree. But his benefits are still a much higher 45% of the big earner’s payouts. In summary? Social Security provides a mild incentive for slacking.

One other factor: after retiring earlier, you might still end up contributing more than you think. This is because any income you earn later in life through optional employment (or self employment) will trigger more contributions. In my 21 years of retirement, I have ended up earning and contributing more during about 15 of those years, bringing my average level up much higher than I originally expected.

Final Tip: If in doubt, ask your Favorite AI.

Even though this has become a long article, it is still far from a complete analysis of the Social Security program. If you want to learn more, I’ve found the AI tools (Anthropic’s Claude, Google Gemini or OpenAI’s Chat GPT) to be shockingly useful at answering questions and running analyses. If you haven’t started using these in your financial research, I highly recommend them. Just search for any of those names (or install the phone app), start typing your questions, and you’ll be learning at a rapid pace within moments.

#56606. The Hidden Benefit Of Being Retired In A Bear Market

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1962 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Financialsamurai ↗ Open Full Page

The Hidden Benefit Of Being Retired In A Bear Market

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, as my public equity portfolio gets obliterated thanks to being overweight tech stocks, I started dusting off my resume to go back to flipping burgers at McDonald’s.
  • Sources indicate that as every long-time investor knows, the name of the game is survival.
  • We're not in an official bear market, yet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, as my public equity portfolio gets obliterated thanks to being overweight tech stocks, I started dusting off my resume to go back to flipping burgers at McDonald’s. Then halfway through the application, I wiped away my tears and took a deep breath.

Sources indicate that as every long-time investor knows, the name of the game is survival. If you can make it through the downturn, good things usually await on the other side.

We're not in an official bear market, yet. But plenty of individual tech names have already fallen by over 20%, and when you're overweight those names, the index's official status doesn't matter much.

So I thought it might be helpful for those who are retired, or who are close, to discuss the positives of going through a downturn. We'll also review how long downturns usually last so we can better prepare.

Recent findings suggest that as the midterm elections demonstrated, a lot of people are not happy with the way our country has been led. But the discontent didn't appear overnight. The stock market was simply acting as a giant dose of Lidocaine.

According to recent reports, as long as stocks kept going up, we could more easily bear higher oil prices, higher food prices, higher housing costs, higher college tuition costs, and explosive medical costs. After all, our investment returns were growing faster than inflation. $6 for a gallon of gas stings a lot less when your brokerage account is up $50,000 for the year.

In a recent development, but that tolerance for rising costs disappears the moment our investments start losing money. Suddenly, $89 a pound for wagyu feels personal.

When the wealth effect vanishes, consumers cut back. Fewer dinners out. Fewer vacations. The new car gets pushed out another year. With declining corporate profitability, companies accelerate layoffs to protect margins. The newly unemployed tighten spending even further.

Rinse and repeat until economists officially declare a recession six months after everybody already felt it.

Sources indicate that if you see the writing on the wall, you want want to get ahead of the layoffs by negotiating your own severance package. If you do, you will probably have an easier time getting a much better exit offer than being lumped with the masses.

If you're newly retired, your biggest fear is sequence of returns risk. That's the risk of suffering big losses early in retirement while you're also withdrawing money to live on. Do that for too long and your portfolio may never recover.

Lose enough and you get forced back to work. Nobody who has tasted freedom wants to return to Monday morning status meetings and performance reviews from someone half their age.

In a recent development, retirees who live off their investments should feel worse about a bear market more than the average worker. We don’t have a paycheck to cushion the blow. We may not have much spare cash flow to buy the dip either.

But here's the key point. If your investments can survive the correction or bear market, you should actually feel good during a downturn. Not ecstatic, but relatively good. Because the alternative is working hard for no financial reward.

How do you know if you can survive? Run through this quick checklist:.

Industry observers note that so how long will the pain last? History offers some comfort, provided you have the patience of a parent waiting for a toddler to put on his shoes while already 15 minutes late.

It has been revealed that according to Capital Group, the S&P 500 has dropped 10% or more about once every 18 months since 1954. A 20%+ bear market reveals up about once every six years.

According to recent reports, in other words, if you plan on a 40-year retirement, expect roughly 25 corrections and six or seven bear markets. Declines are the price of admission, not a sign the world is ending. Get used to them.

Source: Capital Group, S&P 500 data from 1954 through 2025.

It has been revealed that hartford Funds, using Ned Davis Research data going back to 1928, counts 27 bear markets. Stocks fell 35% on average and took 289 days, or about 9.6 months, to hit bottom.

Bear markets were far more common during the Depression era. Since 1945, there have been 15, or one about every 5.1 years.

Industry observers note that two caveats before you get too comfortable. First, these figures measure peak to trough. Getting back to your old high takes longer. Second, the 1973 and 1980 bear markets each dragged on for more than 600 days. Averages are nice until you're living through the outlier.

According to recent reports, but here's the part that should make everyone feel better. Every S&P 500 correction since 1929 has been followed by a recovery, and the average return in the first year after the bottom was 52%. And the recoveries are happening quicker now, if we include the 2025 Liberation Day and 2026 Iran War events.

Sources indicate that hartford also found that about 42% of the S&P 500's strongest days over the past 20 years occurred during bear markets. Sell in a panic and you'll likely miss the rebound.

My takeaway: In a realistic worst-case scenario, blueprint on gutting out roughly 12 to 18 months of pain from peak to trough, with a longer tail to fully recover. That's why the one to two years of cash is fine, especially with interest rates still high.

The existential dilemma of a bear market is this:.

In a recent development, the correct answer is to work less hard and YOLO more. Let me explain using a concept I call Return On Effort (ROE).

Sources indicate that during a bull market, working less hard actually increases your Return On Effort because your investments provide most of the returns. Unless you have a sales job or some other role tightly correlated to performance, an extra 15 hours a week rarely moves the needle. You're better off riding the organization's growth.

During a bear market, working hard to run in place or lose money makes even less sense. There's nothing you can do to stem declining consumer confidence, fresh socialist policies, higher taxes, and so forth. Your boss isn't handing out raises while revenue is falling. See Google's collapse after having such a huge lead in the AI race.

If anything, your extra effort earns you the privilege of doing the work of three colleagues who just got laid off. Congratulations on your 0% raise.

It has been revealed that so you work less hard to protect your declining Return On Effort. Not because you're lazy. Because you're rational.

Recent findings suggest that with this logic in mind, who works the least? The unemployed, the traditional retiree, and the early retiree.

Therefore, so long as your investments can withstand the beating, you're going to be just fine. Psychologically, as a retiree, you must push yourself to do less and have more fun.

Happiness is relative. During a bull market, plenty of early retirees feel a twinge of FOMO watching former colleagues get promoted and cash fat RSU checks. During a bear market, that FOMO flips. Nobody envies the guy grinding through a reorg while his stock comp gets cut in half.

Whether you’re retired or still grinding away, a downturn offers some real perks.

It has been revealed that 1) Things get cheaper. When demand falls, so do prices for travel, hotels, and eventually real estate. Retirees with flexible schedules can travel off-peak and score deals that working parents can only dream about. Workers looking to buy their first home may finally face less competition.

2) You get to shop the sale. Retirees with passive income and a cash buffer get to buy when others are forced to sell. Workers get an even steadier advantage. Every paycheck and 401(k) contribution now picks up more shares at lower prices. Steady income plus a long time horizon makes you the natural buyer in a bear market.

3) Your kids get to buy the dip. I’ve written about how to use stock market downturns to make your kids millionaires. As a father, this is my favorite benefit of a bear market. Because the equity train finally stops long enough for kids to catch up and hop on board. A child has 50+ years of compounding ahead. A 30% drop today is a rounding error by the time they’re in their 50s.

4) Tax moves get better. Tax-loss harvesting offsets future gains. Roth conversions at depressed valuations mean you pay less tax on the same number of shares, and all the recovery happens tax-free.

It has been revealed that 5) The AI hedge is doing its job. Public AI stocks have gotten crunched. But there’s a flip side. If AI companies are struggling to justify their valuations, AI probably isn’t wiping out white-collar work as fast as everyone feared. That’s comforting for our kids, and for every worker wondering if their job will exist in 10 years.

6) You get humbled and build resilience. Being heavily overweight tech felt brilliant for years. Bear markets remind us we’re not as smart as we thought. My advice after every huge win is to go scrub all your toilets. Every downturn you survive makes you a calmer, better investor for the next one. If you’re still working, just make sure your emergency fund is solid, because layoffs tend to show up at the worst time.

You can’t control tech volatility, interest rates, or who wins elections. But you can control how you spend your time during a downturn.

The market will eventually recover. It always has. When it does, the people who grinded through the downturn will be exhausted. Those of us who leaned into family, friends, and fitness will be well rested. Both groups will survive, which is what matters most.

If you’ve been thinking about retiring, a bear market may be the best time to pull the trigger. It means that in spite of the carnage, your finances are strong enough for you to break free. Waiting for the next bull market can feel safer, but it’s backwards.

If your finances can support retirement while stocks are down 20% or more, your plan has already passed the stress test. You’re not retiring on inflated numbers that could vanish in the next correction. And since bear markets don’t last forever, a recovery may carry your retirement forward with a tailwind instead of a headwind.

Compare that to the person who retires at the peak of a bull market, only to watch their portfolio drop 30% in the first two years. That’s sequence of returns risk at its worst.

So go play in the park. Take your kids to the beach. A downturn is the best time to enjoy the freedom you worked so hard to build, and maybe the best time to claim it.

Are you finding it more comforting to be retired during a downturn, or more stressful? How much of your portfolio would need to fall before you'd seriously consider going back to work? Do you agree that working less hard in a bear market is the rational move, or is that just a cop-out for the lazy? And for those still working, has the market selloff made you rethink how hard you're grinding? Are you using the downturn to fund your kids' investment accounts?

According to recent reports, if you want a roadmap for getting through downturns and coming out richer, pick up a copy of Millionaire Milestones: Simple Steps To Seven Figures, a USA Today bestseller. It covers how to keep investing when everybody else is scared, so you can reach financial independence sooner.
