#56529. From Icy Morning to Dead Phone — John Muir Trail Day 22

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (4059 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

From Icy Morning to Dead Phone — John Muir Trail Day 22

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4059 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The night before I dropped down steeply from Donohue Pass.
  • It has been revealed that probably it was warmer there, but that did not mean it was warm!
  • But had it been just a little colder, I would have been overwhelmed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Total Elevation Gain:  48,865 feet.

Pace (minutes per mile):  22:07.

The night before I dropped down steeply from Donohue Pass. In addition to the extra mileage, I also figured it would be warmer at that lower elevation. The camping spot I selected, looking out at a huge golden, grassy meadow, was lovely.

It has been revealed that probably it was warmer there, but that did not mean it was warm! It was already chilly when I went to sleep, and as the night went on it just got colder and colder. I gradually added items to my sleeping bag — sleeping bag liner, long pants, long shirt, puffy hat, gloves — until I used up the entirety of my anti-cold arsenal.

Fortunately, that did the trick. But had it been just a little colder, I would have been overwhelmed. It created a cognitive conflict during my pee errands in the night. My temperature sensors urged me to return to the tent as rapidly as possible. My spiritual-aesthetic soul urged me to spend just a little more time under the glorious blanket of moon and stars.

It has been revealed that towards morning, I had a bizarre dream. It this alternate reality, I was having a hot affair with a woman. Actually, it was a cold affair. Why? Because she was really an alien, part of an extraterrestrial race that was thinking of settling on earth, but who didn’t like our climate. It was too hot for them. Having superior technology, however, they were able to manipulate Earth climate and make it much colder to their liking. So, I was freezing cold, despite having this torrid affair.

Another capability of the alien was that she could make you mostly forget what you had done the night before. So, I kind of knew I was having the affair, but also wasn’t completely sure that I was. The hilarious part was that the alien in the dream was my wife’s friend DG from middle school! When I told Lee about the dream, I had to swear that I had never, ever contemplated having an affair with DG!

Did this moonlight view up through the tent inspire my strange dream?

When it began to get light, I gave myself a little bit of a break because it had been so cold. My last trip outside the tent in the early dawn I looked out on that golden meadow and saw that it was all white, coated with icy rime.

By the time I took this picture, the rime was already melting, but some is still visible.

I also retrieved my bear cannister; it too had a layer of ice on the top cover.

In close-up, the ice on the bear cannister is very visible.

By this I knew it had gone below freezing during the night. So, I allowed myself some extra minutes of warmth in the sleeping bag while I waited for the sun to rise above the lip of the mountains.

I finally got up at 6:30. When the sun came up the temperature rose quickly, but the problem then was that the ice on my tent fly became moisture. Also, the floor was pitched on a sort of pine needle-covered mud. This was very comfortable, but it ended up sticking to my ground sheet. It took some time and effort to get everything dry and clean.

It has been revealed that after all the morning errands, I did not get on the road until – wait for it – ten a.m.! On a short day, that might not have mattered, but I was planning another 17+ miles for this day. The good news was, that I was camped in the Lyell Valley, and the mostly flat trail followed the Lyell Fork river for almost nine miles, all the way to Tuolumne Meadows.

Sometimes the river and trail were close like this, sometimes farther apart.

Industry observers note that with this cruisy route (and my late departure) I turned on the jets as I headed out. With my unfortunate record of falling on easy trails, I was also trying to be careful.

Hard to get lost on this trail!

A good portion of the trail, especially in the meadows, was indented into the earth. My feet were below the ground level in a narrow track. In this configuration, I find that hiking poles are more hazard than help. So, for most of the first nine miles, I was carrying my poles rather than using them.

The statistics tell the tale. Over those nine miles, I was only over 20 minutes (3 mph) twice. My best mile I did in 17:49. That is no record speed, but I don’t think I was even close to that pace anywhere else on the trail.

It has been revealed that the scenery was interesting, but not spectacular. The main thing, with this wide-open valley, was that I could measure my progress visually. I could see an unusual-shaped mountain lining the valley up ahead; then after a time it was closer; then I was opposite to it; and then it was starting to fall behind me. In a slower progression, I could see the distant mountains at the foot of the valley ahead (where the river changes direction). At first, they were far distant, then middle distant, and eventually they were quite close.

The wide glacial valley, filled with meadows, and the mountains at the far end that grew larger as I got closer.

At faster than 3 mph, I was in Tuolumne Meadows in under three hours. As I got closer it was apparent there was a tourist center nearby. Suddenly many more persons were on the trail and most of them were geared out for just a day of hiking or fishing.

The design of Tuolumne was a little weird, with a “downtown” road (Tioga Road) on the north side of the river and a hiking trail parallel on the south side. I generally don’t love road-walking. However, because the Wilderness Center (for permits) was in the middle of downtown, and because I wanted a permit to climb Half Dome the next day, I intended to go via the road.

NPS map of Tuolumne Meadows (in the lower right, I should have turned onto the “National Scenic Trail” but instead stayed on the John Muir Trail).

Recent findings suggest that I missed the turn. Maybe my feet just wanted to stay in the woods? As I realized my error, I ran into a really nice couple who were staying at the fancy lodge nearby. They had a map, and they confirmed, “Yeah, you just have to go back to that last turn and then turn to go across the river, instead of going straight.”.

I had a sudden aversion to that blueprint, particularly because of the miles I wanted to hike that day. The woman must have seen my expression, because she said, “My husband is just like you; he hates to backtrack!”.

In a recent development, it was true. So, I said, “Maybe I’ll go to the Visitor Center instead, and they can help me there.”  I continued on.

It has been revealed that now I was surrounded by roads and parking lots. As I passed one lot, I saw a uniformed ranger manning the booth and I walked up to him. When I explained what I wanted, he mentioned, “First of all, to get a permit, you have to go to the Wilderness Center. Second, they will not give you a permit to climb Half Dome. The only way to get a Half Dome permit is to get a whole different multi-day permit that includes climbing Half Dome within it.”.

Now that had not been my understanding, but he seemed very confident. At this point I was even further away from the Wilderness Center and even less inclined to backtrack. I could see my Half Dome ambitions evaporating. I figured I could still go to the Visitor Center and give it one last try.

Industry observers note that en route I saw that I would pass the market that hosted the famous Tuolumne Grill, and I realized that it was just about lunchtime. I left my pack outside and went in to order. It seemed a simple layout with some picnic tables outside to eat what you ordered. I got a regular hamburger that came with orange juice and some wedge potatoes. The juice tasted delicious on this now-hot day, and the wedges, slathered with ketchup, were good too. But the hamburger? It was an ordinary sort of dry hockey puck, not terrible, but not special at all. I concluded the Grill was famous because of where it was, and not for what it served.

According to recent reports, as I ate it all, I took my phone off of Airplane Mode and called my wife, Lee. (I always hike with it in Airplane Mode to preserve my battery charge.)  When I told her the likely upcoming strategy, without Half Dome, she sounded excited that I was almost done. I was looking forward to seeing her soon as well.

The Visitor Center was a mile-long road walk from there. I had two animal encounters (of a sort) along the way.

According to recent reports, first, I saw wild turkeys! How funny to spend all that time in the wilderness without seeing any (though I did see grouse). Then in congested Tuolumne I saw them. I even got some pictures.

If not for the legs, the turkey blended in….

Second, as I was walking, a car slowed way down opposite me and the driver shouted out his window, “A bear just walked across the road up ahead less than five minutes ago!”.

Sources indicate that I shouted back, “Good! I hope I see him, because I am getting really hungry!”.

Whether he was pulling my leg, or he really saw the bear, I did not see any bear. I was definitely looking out for it though.

Industry observers note that after pine forest and silence, it was disconcerting to walk on asphalt with diesel engines roaring past me. I was glad it was only a mile. On arrival, I went up to the very nice woman in front of the Visitor Center and asked about permits. No surprise, she directed me to the Wilderness Center. I concluded the fates did not intend me to climb Half Dome.

In a recent development, then I asked about getting out of Yosemite when I reached Happy Isles. She explained about the free shuttle within the park that could get me to Curry Village from Happy Isles if I didn’t want to walk there. From Curry Village, the YARTS (Yosemite Area Regional Transportation System) could transport me for a fee. The end of their line was Merced, about three hours away. I figured I could take a train or bus from Merced, or maybe Gabriel could come from Santa Rosa and pick me up there.

Sources indicate that this lady pointed to the YARTS timetable on their bulletin board and suggested I take a picture of it. I replied, “That’s a great idea! You’re a lot smarter than I am to think of it!”.

She also gave me a paper map of the Yosemite Valley to include Happy Isles and Curry Village, saying, “I know you hikers don’t like to add weight, but I think you might find this useful.”.

I told her I was sure I would and stashed it away.

With that, I aimed for the trail, which passed a ways behind the Visitor Center. It was a relief to be walking on pine needles again!

It is funny how swiftly the crowds taper off as you get even a short distance away from the tourist centers.

The other substantial change was in elevation profile. In the morning, the trail had ranged from flat to slightly downhill. Now I would face climbing up past Cathedral Lakes to Cathedral Pass. This was the last pass on the John Muir Trail. It was about 9,700 feet which was a lot lower than the passes in the south, but still more than 1,000 feet above Tuolumne Meadows.

In a recent development, perhaps it was my energy expenditure in the morning, but now I was puffing and panting as I ascended. “Where is my juice?” I asked myself. “This is as bad as climbing Cottonwood Pass on the first day of the JMT!”.

I was breathing hard, but enjoying the enormous granite rock.

Sources indicate that the inspiration was the views. There was more than one rocky shape that could qualify as a “cathedral.”  Imagine Notre Dame. Imagine that the roof is one thousand feet high, the spires soar over 1,500 feet, and the nave stretch two miles. Then imagine a landscape dotted with two or three of these behemoths. It was magical.

About the time my legs finally got warmed up, I came across a couple that were on the first day of their John Muir Trail hike. The reversal I had imagined, when encountering near-finishers at the start of my own hike, was coming true. In chatting, he warned me, “Oh, there’s no water except at Upper Cathedral.”.

In a recent development, I appreciated that intel and was on the lookout for a spot near Upper Cathedral Creek. As I ascended, coming above the tree line, I was surprised not to find it. Then, as I passed a quarter mile from Upper Cathedral Lake, I saw some people emerge on a trail from the lake onto the main trail. Suddenly it dawned on me that there was no creek. He meant the lake!

Sources indicate that it was late afternoon and I wanted to press on and find a campsite. But if this was really “last water” it would be foolish not to take the detour for it.

Industry observers note that the lake seemed to have mostly marshy and muddy access points. These would entail wet feet and dirty water to filter. However, I saw a rocky promontory jutting into the lake where a bunch of guys were hanging out. I headed there to refill my water.

It has been revealed that I began chatting with them and learned they were from Kansas City. I asked them whether they lived in Kansas or Missouri and they stated that only someone who knows Kansas City would ask that question. I explained that I had a cousin who lived in K.C. and they told me they lived on the Kansas side.

Industry observers note that overall, they were nice enough, but the banter occasionally felt a little mocking. For example, they asked me, “Did you go up Whitney?”   I replied that I had, but that I had been fighting a respiratory infection, making it very difficult.

In a recent development, they responded, “Oh, that just adds to your story about climbing Mount Whitney. Like, ‘everybody else just climbed it, but I climbed it with a respiratory infection, coughing every step of the way!’”.

They were actually not wrong, but the tone felt a little snarky.

It has been revealed that after I filled both my water bottles and my Katadyn BeFree to have maximum water available, I headed back toward the trail. One of the guys, maybe the leader, followed me a short distance and called me over. He was asking me about the trail, and it turned out he had done the trail himself a few years before. It seemed a little odd, but I took him as just wanting to reminisce a bit about his own experience.

In a recent development, in a quarter mile I was back at the junction with the JMT. The beauty of the scenery around Cathedral Lakes is so inspiring, I wanted to take some more pictures. John Muir himself mentioned, on summiting Cathedral Peak, “This I may say is the first time I have been at church in California, led here at last, every door graciously opened for the poor lonely worshiper.”  (Quoted from My First Summer in the Sierra, Chapter 10, entry for September 7, 1869.).

In a recent development, so, this “lonely worshiper” reached for his smart phone to capture the majestic giants and discovered… nothing. Nothing at all, a black screen. Now my eyesight is not great without glasses, but I had thought my phone showed 65% of charge when last I checked.

In case it had just shut off for some reason, I tried to restart it, but still nothing. I was crestfallen, thinking, “Oh no! My phone died here on the trail with barely one day left on my hike!!!”.

Sources indicate that I could not fathom how it happened. I had not dropped it that I could recall. Deeply disappointed, I began having paranoid thoughts. “If I had charge, and now suddenly I don’t, could that guy who followed me, to talk to me, have had some technology that fried my phone? Like some super magnet or something?”.

It seemed wildly implausible, but the coincidence – that it happened right after our exchange – seemed strange.

According to recent reports, then I calmed down somewhat. I reminded myself of what was truly vital,  “This trip is about the experience itself. It is not ultimately about telling the story or capturing the pictures, it is about your lived experience.”.

According to recent reports, seen through that prism my loss was minor and I settled down. My wife and I always try to distinguish “disappointments” from “tragedies,” and this was clearly the former.

Industry observers note that with the light turning to a mellow glow in the sky, I continued hiking. Cathedral Pass was not much further. It was unusual, in that the trail reached the pass, but did not descend from there down the other side. Instead, it continued on, ascending further up the ridge of one of the mountainsides bordering the pass.

According to recent reports, now my lack of a phone was frustrating because I had lost my navigation device. I was not sure how far I should ideally go before selecting a camp, remembering that I wanted to make miles to ensure I could finish on the following day.

It has been revealed that the mountains answered that question for me. As I continued higher, I came to a turn on the outstretched flank of the range. Extending from the trail was a large flat spot, with visibility in all directions. The ground was ideal for pitching a tent. The views were magical in the waning light. I thought, “I can go further, and shorten my day tomorrow. Or I can camp tonight in the most beautiful spot in the Sierras.”  That decision was an easy one.

In a recent development, in Tuolumne I heard we were in for another icy night, and I was now at a higher elevation than I had been the night before. So, I was expecting cold. In fact, as the sun dropped behind the peaks, I could feel the chill almost immediately.

Sources indicate that I started to pitch my tent, and maybe I was in too much of a hurry? I love my Massive Agnes TigerWall, but on this night, as I tried to get a pole into the slot, the pole snapped. After the dead phone, this might have been a devastating blow. But in this stunning location, on the last night I needed a tent, it did not phase me. Besides, I had been carrying a seemingly useless stupid little tube for miles and miles, wondering why I bothered, and now I had my answer. I slid the tube over the broken spot, taped it in place with surgical tape (though that might have been unnecessary), and reseated the pole in the slot. Good as new? Maybe not, but close enough.

According to recent reports, having pitched my tent, I just basked in the beauty of the location for a few minutes. Then I soaked my food and found a spot for a cat hole and dug what was likely to be my last cat hole on the trail. The cold soak did not take long, but the result was the opposite of the previous night’s dinner. That food had not rehydrated fully but was wonderfully seasoned and tasted delicious. This night the mashed potatoes and chicken hydrated easily, but they were totally bland. They didn’t taste bad really, they just didn’t taste like anything at all!

Of course, mindful as always that this is fuel first and flavor second, I wolfed it all down.

It has been revealed that with no phone, I was communicating with my family by Garmin. That was so onerous, typing out everything, one letter at a time. (On the trail I learned of an app that makes this easier, but I didn’t have either the app or a working phone.)  Gabriel seemed amenable to picking me up in Merced, and so I realized I needed to make substantial speed the next day to get to Happy Isles. The 4:50 p.m. YARTS departure to Merced arrived by 8:30 p.m. Even that would mean getting back to Santa Rosa by midnight, after all. Our back and forth about this on the Garmin was practically in code, but I thought the initiative was set.

Wrapping up my chores in deep twilight, I stored everything in my bear cannister and – why not? — I hooked my phone to the charger.

It has been revealed that before going to sleep, I decided to just take a peek at the phone. What?? Yes! Yes!! My phone was charging!!!

Sources indicate that I was elated and still baffled as to how it happened. I could not be sure. The best explanation I came up with was this:  First, without my glasses I had misread the charge level on the phone. It did not have 65%, it must have had much less. Second, after speaking with my wife from the restaurant at lunch, I must not have turned Airplane Mode back on, so that the phone drained far more rapidly in the afternoon than it did in the morning. That is my best guess. Operator error.

The most beautiful campsite — taken under the stars, after my phone revived.

Snuggled in my tent, I got gussied up, wearing all of my clothing in preparation for a second icy cold night.

My tent in the moonlight of the last night — repaired and welcoming (except for the mess inside!).

Industry observers note that it boggled my mind to think that – most probably – I was wrapped in my sleeping bag for the last time this year. The excitement of (hopefully) completing the trail the next day would normally have kept me wide awake. But no. I was just too tired and slept right away.

It has been revealed that hi, I’m Papa George! In my 69 years I’ve done a lot of cool things – I’ve crossed the Atlantic in a 40-foot sailboat, bushwacked 100 miles across the north slope of the Alaska Range, hiked for 26 days in Western Nepal crossing five passes over 5,000 meters, and climbed Mt. Kilimanjaro, to name a few. It was my honor to serve my country as a diplomat around the world for 34 years. I have been active in retirement, and I hiked the Wonderland Trail in 2024 and the Long Trail in 2025. This year I'm trying... the John Muir Trail!

In a recent development, enjoying the tales from the trail. I flashed back to moment playing volleyball the first week of freshman college out of state, people ask where they’re from, and the guy from kansas city asked me what state I thought he was from. Kansas? He was so miffed.

Notify me via e-mail if anyone answers my comment.

Winners of the Banff Mountain Film Festival Announced

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (801 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the annual Banff Centre Mountain Festival gathers mountain luminaries from across the world at the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity in Alberta.
  • Industry observers note that the Grand Prize went to Listen, directed by Taliesin Black-Brown.
  • Rose Bush, an Oscar Award-winning director of photography serving on the competition’s jury, called Listen “a film that engages human-caused environmental devastation — the existential dilemma of our time — at its nucleus with overwhelming love and hope.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the annual Banff Centre Mountain Festival gathers mountain luminaries from across the world at the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity in Alberta. There, a celebration of mountain culture recognizes the best outdoor films and books of the past year. The climax of the festival took place this past weekend, and the winners of the 51st annual Banff Mountain Film Competition have now been announced.

Industry observers note that the Grand Prize went to Listen, directed by Taliesin Black-Brown. In this short documentary, sound engineer Hank Lentfer records the sounds of nature around his Alaska home, while caring for his mother with dementia. As Lentfer documents the degradation of the natural world, we witness the slow loss of his mother. Drawing together these two threads, the film explores connection despite, and through, loss, using sound.

Rose Bush, an Oscar Award-winning director of photography serving on the competition’s jury, called Listen “a film that engages human-caused environmental devastation — the existential dilemma of our time — at its nucleus with overwhelming love and hope.”.

The film also won the Grand Jury Prize at the Tribeca Film Festival.

In addition to a grand prize, the festival honors films in several categories. The winning film in the Adventure category was The Navigator, a feature-length work from director Jordan Manley. The film follows Nainoa Thompson, who was the first Native Hawaiian in six centuries to make the journey from Hawaii to Tahiti in a traditional voyaging canoe. Now, almost five decades later, Thompson and his crew make the journey again, using only traditional navigation techniques.

The best film in the Mountain Culture category was Land of Canaan, produced and directed by Maggie Lemere. Lemere’s film follows a group of Palestinian olive farmers, who work to protect their ancient olive groves amid the destruction by Israel. The film “illuminated the vital relationship of courage, vision, hope, and traditional ecological knowledge,” juror Rose Bush mentioned, “in service of the essential value of sovereignty via mountain culture.”.

In a recent development, in the Environment category, director James Dawson’s winning comedic documentary Derek vs Derek follows two Devon farmers, both named Derek. One Derek is an ardent dairy farmer while his environmentalist neighbor begins rewilding his land. A feud naturally ensues.

According to recent reports, the Arc’teryx-sponsored Best Climbing Film was Zindabad, directed by Tom Fish. Fish follows Pakistani climber Mueez Ud Din into the Karakoram, alongside his uncle Javed Ali and French climber Mathieu Maynadier. Ud Din explores a remote, unknown glacier system, while the film examines what it means to be a Pakistani climber among peaks long claimed by international outsiders.

Industry observers note that directed by Alexis Berg, the Mountain Sports winner, Roots, follows trail runner Ruth Croft as she examines her future as an elite ultra-trail runner after an injury. Roots is “about an inner journey of healing and acceptance, rooted in the essential joy of running outdoors,” explained juror David Arnaud.

In a recent development, the Snow Sports winner centers on American skier Jessie Diggins. Diggins is the most decorated American cross-country skier ever, but Threshold, directed by Torsten Brinkema, reveals the deep personal struggles behind that success. Juror Beki Henderson noted that “the jury particularly commends Jessie Diggins for her extraordinary courage and honesty in sharing her story.”.

There were more mountain films this year than you can even imagine. With 610 film submissions and 83 finalists, it’s no wonder that there are still more category winners.

Recent findings suggest that best short film winner Hello, Beautiful follows climber Alannah Yip as she struggles with identity, training for the Olympics while enduring medical hair loss. Director Darcy Hennessey created a film which “reminds us that personal transformation does not always come from pushing harder,” juror Kerry Stauffer explained.

For best feature film, the competition announced Ceremony, directed and produced by Banchi Hanuse. The film tells the story of the disappearance of the ooligan, a small fish, from British Columbia’s Bella Coola River. Jurors praised the film’s use of watercolor animation, personal stories, and community broadcasts to explore the importance of a seemingly unimportant little fish.

Director Marco Tribelhorn’s 75 seconds won the Creative Excellence Award. The film documents free-skier Jacob Wester’s 75-second-long battle for survival while trapped in an avalanche.

“A compelling visual treatment brings to life an experience that is impossible to imagine,” said Kerry Stauffer.

According to recent reports, last but not least, the Audience Choice Award went to Only Music // Snake River. Director Justin Fountain’s documentary follows a band that ditches the tour bus for a journey down the Snake River, seeking connection with strangers.

According to recent reports, tickets for the international film festival are now available. We have also covered the recently confirmed Banff Mountain Book Award winners.

A 3,300Km Walk Across Japan in Winter

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (474 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Japanese publisher Katsunari Tanaka has set himself the challenge of hauling a handcart 3,345km from Japan’s northernmost tip to the southern edge of Okinawa in winter.
  • Tanaka, 49, set off from Cape Sōya in Hokkaido on October 7 and is heading south to Cape Hedo in Okinawa.
  • Rather than carrying everything on his back, he is pulling a handcart that weighs around 100kg.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Japanese publisher Katsunari Tanaka has set himself the challenge of hauling a handcart 3,345km from Japan’s northernmost tip to the southern edge of Okinawa in winter.

Tanaka, 49, set off from Cape Sōya in Hokkaido on October 7 and is heading south to Cape Hedo in Okinawa. He hopes to complete the traverse in 100 days over five months. As he will have to contend with some challenging winter conditions along the way, he has described it as “playing chase with winter.”.

Rather than carrying everything on his back, he is pulling a handcart that weighs around 100kg. He also has a support team with a vehicle in case of emergencies. At some points, different members of his team have walked with him for a day or so. His daily target is around 35km, with rest days and organized stops built into the schedule.

Industry observers note that the first few weeks have already brought strong headwinds, rain, and some steep climbs, making progress difficult at times. Temperatures have dropped close to freezing. At the end of October, he crossed a mountain pass between Yoichi and Iwanai. There, headwinds stirred up the gravel as he walked. Then the snow began. In the end, he took refuge with his support team until the weather improved.

Industry observers note that despite the conditions, Tanaka reached Hakodate Harbor on November 3, having covered 621km across Hokkaido. From Hakodate, he is crossing the Tsugaru Strait by ferry to Aomori, then will continue south along the Sanriku coast to Sendai.

From there, he follows the Pacific coast through Fukushima to Tokyo before joining the Tokaido route toward Osaka before heading west to Kyushu. A second ferry crossing brings him to Okinawa, where he will walk to his final destination, Cape Hedo.

Recent findings suggest that along a road in Hokkaido. Photo: Katsunari Tanaka/Instagram.

This is not Tanaka’s first experience of traveling Japan with a handcart. Around a decade ago, he spent three years visiting all 47 prefectures, selling books directly to people he met along the way. Loading his publications onto a cart, he covered the country between 2013 and 2016, eventually selling 13,477 books. At the time, many people questioned what he was doing and whether books could really be sold on the street. But he notes the experience shaped his approach to business and his belief in the power of personal connections.

Tanaka insists that he is not an adventurer. Instead, he is traveling the country as a “merchant.” This time, he is making the journey to support his mentor, Arthur Hollands, a Japanese evangelist known for undertaking lengthy walks while carrying a large wooden cross. Along the route, Tanaka plans to stop at 11 locations to give lectures. He welcomes people to join him for sections of the walk.

Photo: Katsunari Tanaka/Instagram.

First Ski Descent of Meru Central

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (421 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tiphaine Duperier and Boris Langenstein of France have notched another Himalayan first ski descent, this time down the southwest face of Meru Central (6,310m) in India’s Garhwal Himalaya.
  • Duperier admitted they started the expedition with low expectations after several projects earlier in the fall all failed.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Snow conditions had been unforgiving,” she wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tiphaine Duperier and Boris Langenstein of France have notched another Himalayan first ski descent, this time down the southwest face of Meru Central (6,310m) in India’s Garhwal Himalaya. The skiers are still surprised by how lucky they were.

Duperier admitted they started the expedition with low expectations after several projects earlier in the fall all failed.

Recent findings suggest that “Snow conditions had been unforgiving,” she wrote. “We figured there was only a 3-in-10 chance of skiing the southwest face of Meru.”.

But when they got there, the mountain was, they added, “generous” with them.

Recent findings suggest that the three-peaked Meru massif, located in the Gangotri Glacier region of the Garhwal Himalaya, lies between Shivling and Thalay Sagar. It has three peaks: 6,660m Meru South, 6,310m Meru Central, and 6,450m Meru North. The ski descent line is in purple. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein.

“We spent six days of reconnaissance and three [days] climbing the peak, [thanks to] an unprecedented stroke of luck in finding a way through the icefall and perfect snow in the upper section,” she explained.

Industry observers note that the icefall on Meru Central. Photo: Boris Langenstein.

The icefall at the base of the peak was indeed one of the most complex passages. The pair climbed a 15m pitch of WI4 and left a safety rope, which they also used to rappel down after the ski descent, Duperier told PlanetMountain.

Recent findings suggest that otherwise, the pair of regular expedition and skiing partners climbed alpine-style and pretty fast, reaching the summit in less than eight hours. According to their research, they completed the second-ever ascent of the southwest face of Meru, after an Indian team in 2023.

Recent findings suggest that at the summit on Meru Central. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein.

Industry observers note that the skiers estimate they covered 1,500m on their descent, with some sections reaching 50 °. Snow conditions were good overall, hard but with a good grip.

“We skied like little monkeys on the wires in Rishikesh,” Duperier posted on social media. “It was just incredible, truly beautiful!”.

While the climbers rappelled down the icefall onto the glacier below, the ski descent itself had no rappels or interruptions.

Duperier barely had time to return home to France to pick up a Piolet d’Or for the first alpine-style ascent of the Schell Route on the Rupal Face of Nanga Parbat, followed by the first ski descent from the 8,125m summit.

In a recent development, tiphaine Duperier at the Piolets d’Or ceremony. Photo: Piotr Drozdz.

Tech Report: Swatara Treasure Hunt

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1500 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I battle rocks and falling temperatures while searching for a lost item on trail.
  • Recent findings suggest that my looks are rarely flexible, until they are.
  • In a recent development, I texted my change in plans to Pebbles as I made my way down the trail.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I battle rocks and falling temperatures while searching for a lost item on trail.

Recent findings suggest that my looks are rarely flexible, until they are. I checked in with Pebbles last night to see what she, Rebar, and Greasetrap had planned (Soaked completed his hike the previous day, huge congrats to him!). They planned to slack-packing 15 miles starting from Swatara Gap and heading south. I would be doing the same – but I had the section heading north scheduled first. Not a significant deal, I could just swap them. However, my section south of Swatara Gap called for 24 miles of hiking. I would need to start early and hike flat out all day to make it before sunset. I knew that isn’t really their style, which is valid. I had made up my mind and was sticking to my plan. I was up early and decided to head towards town to buy a coffee. While enjoying my hot beverage in my car I decided to take one last look at both itineraries. I might not be able to hike with them, but simply flipping my current section might allow me to pass them early in the day. Eventually I have to earn my trail name, right? I set a course for Swatara Gap and was on trail close to 8:00AM.

In a recent development, I texted my change in plans to Pebbles as I made my way down the trail. No sooner had I switched my phone into airplane mode and put it back in my pack than 3 hikers appeared ahead. Ca-caw! The group chimed. Ca-caw! I called back. Soon we were catching up and discussing our future hiking plans and Rebars new kicks. His previous Altras had taken a beating on the trail, I recall him putting some kind of indestructible adhesive on them during a previous encounter. He now had a snazzy new pair of Altras and was clearly enjoying the upgrade. After chatting for a few minutes we agreed to keep in close contact since I’ll soon be skipping ahead of them to close out my hike. The trail crosses the Swatara Creek on the 19th century Waterville Bridge, an interesting piece of industrial era engineering.

In a recent development, as I approached the bridge, I felt my phone vibrate. I had left it on since I had parked my car in a lot that requires calling the state park if you intend to leave your vehicle there overnight. I thought I might get a call back since I left a message. Instead I saw that it was Pebbles calling me. “So, you know how you like treasure hunts? Well, Rebar left a dry bag at the last campsite…”. For the third time, I was going to help the crew out by retrieving an object they’d left behind. I think I could make a living doing this professionally given the dozens of items reported missing on FarOut. Drive to the nearest trailhead, hike out and retrieve the item, drive it up the trail or ship it back to its owner, profit. Of course, for friends I’ll stick with the rate of a few guava candies. A few miles later I was staring at a bag resting neatly by a fire pit, it was definitely Rebar’s, my easiest find yet!

The trail had leveled off onto another long ridge, but the rocks made sure things weren’t too easy for me. The rocks and cold became the theme of the day. I had endured many cold days but not one single time had I ended a day with my sleeping layers still on. Hiking always warmed me up a ton and often after 30-minutes of hiking I’d shed them and hike in my shorts and sun hoodie. The climb out of Swatara Gap warmed me up and had me considering stopping to make the adjustment. But I wanted to see how I felt once the climbing stopped and I was just moving along the mostly level ridge. My temperature returned to a comfortable level promptly, so I was content to keep moving and keep the layers on. There were a handful of views along the ridge, but otherwise minimal points of interest aside from some boulder fields.

Classic Pennsylvania ridge rocks.

Looking south from the ridge north of Swatara Gap.

Looking south from the ridge north of Swatara Gap.

Looking south from the ridge north of Swatara Gap.

Looking south from the ridge north of Swatara Gap.

Eventually I came to Route 501. I considered taking the path to the 501 Shelter, but the comments on FarOut mentioned it was boarded up with no facilities for hikers. That didn’t sound worth documenting for the blog so I continued along the AT a few miles to the Showers Steps viewpoint. It was a gorgeous view, but unlike many of the viewpoints from the ridges I have been hiking along it faced the sunset. It was cloudy, but there were signs that some semblance of a sunset might be visible. A few breaks in the clouds, tunnels of light illuminating small areas of the valley below. I hadn’t planned to camp here, but a check of FarOut revealed that I had just enough time to hike to Route 183 and back if I really hauled. There were more viewpoints ahead so I decided to check those out and make a decision along the way.

The trail traded rocky sections with cruisy for the next few miles. Each viewpoint I passed faced too far toward the east to offer a view of the sunset. They probably would have been great for sunrise, but it was supposed to be cloudy. Sunrise would be a total question mark as to whether there would be much to see. Today’s sunset at least had a little promise. In fact, the beams of sun were occasionally shining on the trail, I felt external warmth for the first time all day. Was it a sign that I should camp at Showers Steps? I figured that was the best blueprint and hurried down the trail.

On my way back I stopped at the Hertlein Creek to collect water for the evening. I stopped at the first trickle of water, which meant I missed seeing the nearby campsites and swimming hole complete with rope swing. It probably wasn’t the right weather for the latter but it would have been cool to have a quick look-see.

Industry observers note that I was back at the Showers Steps in time for sunset, but I could tell the whole way back that was not really going to be much to see. The clouds had rolled back in, some quite dark. The view was still great, just not quite what I’d hustled for. I pitched my tent near a makeshift shelter, noticing that, by some miracle, my tent was already mostly dry. The rain two nights ago had soaked it, I expected a long wait for it dry out in the 40 degree weather, but was pleasantly surprised that I could go right ahead and set up my bed for the night. Soon I was bracing for the night, which was going be perhaps the coldest night I’ve spent in my tent all year.

More of Pennsylvania’s “state flower”.

A memorial to William F. Shanaman near the Showers Steps.

The view from Showers Steps in the early afternoon.

A cruisy and photogenic section of the trail.

Looking west from the trail near Hertlein Creek.

Decent and collectable flow at Hertlein Creek.

Looking west from the trail near Hertlein Creek.

Looking west from the trail near Hertlein Creek.

The best use of Pennsylvania rocks I’ve seen so far. You could be one of these every 10 feet.

Pleased with this pitch, not an easy feat in a pile of rocks.

Total: 27.6 miles, 55,557 steps.

The buyer pays the same price as they would otherwise, and your purchase helps to support The Trek's ongoing goal to serve you quality backpacking advice and information. Thanks for your support!

To learn more, please visit the About This Site page.

Sources indicate that I’m See You Tomorrow (SYT), a 30-something hiker who loves hiking just for the thrill of seeing things that most people don’t. I have no problem eating the same things every day and, for me, over-analyzing everything is half the fun (sometimes more). I am new to backpacking but that won’t stop me from taking on an unorthodox hike of the Appalachian Trail in 2026. It’s not quite a yo-yo, but I have aspirations of hiking the entire trail twice in one year. For the rest of the story you’ll just have to start reading my blog!

Arctic Town Kills Dozens of Grizzlies Feeding on Dump

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (318 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For years, the grizzlies near Inuvik in Canada’s western Arctic relied on a stable source of food — the town dump.
  • In 2025, before the fence was built, trail cameras captured multiple grizzlies hanging around the dump, looking for food.
  • In a recent development, it was too much.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For years, the grizzlies near Inuvik in Canada’s western Arctic relied on a stable source of food — the town dump. Generations of bears grew up feeding there. In 2025, wildlife officials found that over 40 grizzlies regularly visited the dump.

In 2025, before the fence was built, trail cameras captured multiple grizzlies hanging around the dump, looking for food. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories.

In a recent development, it was too much. This year, the town built an electric fence around the site, hoping the bears would move on. They didn’t. Some started coming into town looking for food. Others just hung around the fence, searching for a way in.

It has been revealed that “They would just do these laps around the dump, and they would just be emaciated, sickly,” mentioned Toby Halle, a Renewable Resources officer based in Inuvik, told the CBC. “They don’t know what to do with themselves. And quite frankly, we don’t know what to do with them.”.

Inuvik, population about 3,500, was the first community in that part of the Arctic to try to wean the bears off their dependence on dump food with such a fence, which cost about $700,000. The problem was, the bears had not learned to depend on any other source of food.

According to recent reports, “We’ve probably had three to four generations of bears that have been using that landfill,” said local mayor Peter Clarkson. In the end, the town took a drastic solution — but one that was probably unavoidable in the circumstances: They shot 28 bears.

Tragic though this is, officials hope that within the next couple of years, the remaining bears in the area will move on and learn to eat more natural fare.

Industry observers note that many other Arctic towns still have open dumps where bears come to feed. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories.

#56523. Tech Report: Leonard Clark: Explorer, Spy, Liar

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2563 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Leonard Clark: Explorer, Spy, Liar

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2563 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Born in 1907, Leonard Francis Clark was an explorer, war hero, and writer who made daring expeditions all over the world before dying mysteriously in Venezuela in 1957.
  • According to recent reports, today, he isn’t well known, but has this lack of scrutiny been a blessing in disguise for this forgotten explorer’s legacy?
  • According to recent reports, A Tibetan expedition under Leonard Clark in 1949.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Born in 1907, Leonard Francis Clark was an explorer, war hero, and writer who made daring expeditions all over the world before dying mysteriously in Venezuela in 1957.

According to recent reports, today, he isn’t well known, but has this lack of scrutiny been a blessing in disguise for this forgotten explorer’s legacy? His books, filled with adventure and excitement, read like fiction. The more one digs into the forgotten reports and old newspaper articles, the stranger his story, and the more complicated the man.

According to recent reports, A Tibetan expedition under Leonard Clark in 1949. Photo: The Marching Wind.

Recent findings suggest that the main sources on Leonard Clark are all, well, Leonard Clark. This isn’t necessarily damning, but it is something he shares with most good con artists or cult leaders. The following is a short biography based only on official records, such as draft cards and census data. The first rule of reading historical accounts is that every historical figure is a liar.

Leonard Francis Clark was born in British Columbia, Canada, in January 1907 to two Americans, Maud and Francis Clark. In 1909, they moved back to Maud’s birth state of California, and Francis promptly died.

Industry observers note that there are conflicting statements online about which university he attended, but census data highlights him living only a few kilometers from the University of California (now the University of California, Berkeley) in 1930, so I’d put my money on that one. He began traveling right out of college, spending three years in Borneo on a hunting trip with his brother, Laurence. By the late 1930s, he was on a National Geographic-funded expedition to the South China Sea.

Photo: National Geographic Archives.

Sources indicate that his article, cryptically titled Among the Big Knot Lois of Hainan, was published in the 1938 September edition. In it, he recounts how he and a small expeditionary force landed in the midst of a deadly cholera epidemic. Relying on hired porters to carry their supplies, Clark and Nicol Smith, another future travel writer, set off into the interior. Soon, malaria and infection laid low most of the team, including, per Clark’s article, Smith.

Again, according to Clark, Smith urged him to take the remaining five porters, the minimum of equipment, and keep going.

Much of the article is dedicated to ethnographic observations, with the typical exoticism and patronizing tone of the era. At one point, Clark noted that the Li people of Hainan reminded him of indigenous Amazonian people and “the men were tall, many six feet.”.

Sources indicate that A recent study indicated that the average height for men in Hainan today is 168.7cm, around 5’6″, and the same study found that average heights had increased over the past century. This is a small nitpick, but he’ll repeat this unlikely claim again in the Amazon. It is worth noting that the “six-foot-tall Indian warrior” was a stock character in contemporary pulp adventure fiction.

In a recent development, there is an interesting contrast between Clark’s account and some of the newspaper reports, especially one from a Virginia paper, which relied on Smith for the story. This article implies Smith did much more than lay around his tent with malaria. Clark’s article claims he was the first white man to enter 47 different villages, while the newspaper says that Smith was the first Westerner to penetrate inland.

There is a third source: the 37-minute silent film compiled from the expedition’s footage and photographs. In it, we briefly see a white man lying under a mosquito net as if ill. But whether this is Smith, Clark — who admits himself to experiencing malaria symptoms on the expedition — or the third westerner on the expedition, one Jack Munroe, the film doesn’t say.

Photo: National Geographic Archive.

His previous experience in the region led him to return a few years later, this time on behalf of the U.S. Office of Strategic Services (OSS), a precursor to the CIA. His work during the war centered around the China-Burma-India corridor, particularly the Yellow River valley. He was involved in organizing guerrilla activities, building intelligence networks, and navigating the Japanese surrender of Taiwan.

In a later press statement, Clark explained how he had worked with General Dai Li, and that “the Reds had it in for him,” due to the infamously repressive actions Dai Li took against Chinese Communists. Dai Li, whom historian Barbara Tuchman called “China’s combination of Himmler and J. Edgar Hoover,” was killed in a 1946 plane crash. Wide speculation places the blame for this crash on either the Chinese Communist Party or the OSS. This would make things awkward for Clark a few years later.

According to recent reports, he continued his government work in the area after the Second World War, sliding right into the developing Cold War. In 1949, Clark led a large, well-funded expedition into Tibet.

It would have gotten him in the history books if Leonard Clark identified a peak higher than Everest. Unfortunately for him, he didn’t. But he certainly proposed that he had, when he claimed that he’d surveyed Amne Machin and found it to be 9,040m high.

Recent findings suggest that amne Machin is not taller than Everest. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

Clark published his account of the expedition years later, titled The Marching Wind. In it, he wrote with his typical style: daring escapes, stereotypically aggressive natives, and breezy adventure writing. What it did not contain was the data to support his claims.

Sources indicate that as soon as he released his first report and measurements, geographers, geologists, and mountaineers pored over them. Bradford Washburn, a cartographer, photographer, and explorer, published a thorough examination of the surveying techniques and questionable results from Clark’s expedition.

A contemporary review in the Alpine Journal, commenting on his photographic evidence, wrote that “anything more unconvincing could hardly be imagined — yet, ostensibly…the mountain was the object of the expedition.” More on that “ostensibly” later. Suffice it to say, Clark’s estimate that Amne Machin could be almost 1,000m taller than Everest was not adopted by geographers at large.

Recent findings suggest that the review concluded that “it can hardly be wondered if mountaineers, whom Mr. Clark rather despises, cannot accept his results.”.

Clark blithely remarked that he had “some rather bulky complaints by mountain and other specialists,” but admitted subpar instruments made his results “indecisive.”.

Industry observers note that A surveying party including Clark, far right, taking observations of Amne Machin. Photo: The Marching Wind.

It has been revealed that if he doesn’t seem too broken up, it may be because Amne Machin’s height wasn’t the main purpose of his trip. Clark was supported logistically and went on behalf of Ma Bufang, the fiercely anti-communist warlord ruling Qinghai, on the border of Tibet. Anticipating that he could not long hold out against the People’s Liberation Army, Clark proposed that his expedition would map a path of retreat. This would help Ma Bufang’s army cross into Tibet and continue their anti-Communist campaign from the mountains.

Clark envisioned Ma Bufang’s Qinghai, through Tibet, becoming “the bulwark against Red invasion of India.” Clark went on the expedition and did his mapping, but the PLA took Qinghai only months later, and Ma Bufang fled to Hong Kong.

Recent findings suggest that in his introduction to his book, Clark claims that the United States was unaware of his “very slight aid” to Ma Bufang and local anti-Communist guerrilla activities, and he involved himself with the Chinese Nationalist army “as a private American citizen.” If I were to say that I was skeptical of this claim, I would not be the first to do so. But that falls under speculation, so I will say only that I sent a Freedom of Information Act request to the CIA regarding Clark’s work in Tibet. However, the records were not forthcoming.

After returning from the mountains, Clark went to a wedding anniversary celebration in Canton, surrounded by his fellow Allied intelligence members and their set. Things got a little out of hand, and Clark soon found himself in a Cantonese jail with a bullet wound and two manslaughter charges.

According to recent reports, chinese Nationalist soldiers on Clark’s Tibetan expedition. Photo: The Marching Wind.

The other two men involved were Harold Harris, an Englishman who died immediately, and Willard Freeman from Massachusetts, who died later from his injuries. Clark also sustained a gunshot wound, but had recovered sufficiently by late November to be moved from hospital to prison.

The three had been drinking together in Freeman’s home when, at about 4 am, servants reported hearing gunshots. Mrs. Maya Freeman entered the room at 10 am to find an odd and grisly scene. Harris, fully clothed, lay dead on Freeman’s bed with three gunshot wounds. Freeman, completely nude, was also lying on the bed, alive with two shots to the abdomen. Clark, in his underwear, was on a second bed, with a single gunshot to the chest. Furniture was overturned, indicating a fight, and all three were covered in scratches. The only weapon found was Clark’s .32 caliber pistol.

In a recent development, later that month, the Canton District Court denied Clark’s bail request. The court, still trying to determine what exactly happened, focused on the widowed Maya Freeman. Interviewing her for hours, they attempted to make her confess to an affair with Clark. Both of them repeatedly denied it. Clark further denied that he had fired any of the six shots, though he didn’t name the shooter.

Clark’s brother contacted former OSS head General William Donovan, who rallied the State Department. Clark reportedly was concerned that if he wasn’t released before the city fell to the Communists, he would be tortured for information regarding Dai Li and OSS activities. The State Department investigated and, thanks to its intervention, Clark was released.

Clark’s legal troubles were splashed across newspapers worldwide. Photo: The Journal (Caldwell, Ohio) November 24, 1949.

What exactly happened in Freeman’s house that night? Was the dispute between the Allied Intelligence men personal, or professional? If the world were ever to find out, it wouldn’t be from Clark. Once freed, Clark returned to California and moved on to his next adventure. It was an ambitious one: Leonard Clark was going to discover the lost city of El Dorado.

He had an old parchment map to the lost city, he claimed, which revealed it lay in the upper reaches of Peru. Never mind that it had been pretty well established for over a century that El Dorado was a myth, following the efforts of explorers Alexander von Humboldt and Robert Schomburgk.

It has been revealed that clark’s resulting account, The Rivers Ran East, contains all the genre tropes you would expect from a fictional work in the same setting. Native Amazonians are ferocious cannibals who capture Clark and keep him in a poison snake pit, crocodiles can and must be lassoed (there are no crocodiles in Peru, only caimans, a type of alligator), and there is a beautiful lady explorer, Inez Pokorny, who is secretly part of a London-based international El Dorado-seeking organization. If this organization existed, I have found no trace of it outside of this book.

If I were to list every blatant impossibility in his account, we would be here for days, so I’ll just continue on one particular thread: Leonard Clark seems to have a very loose grasp of which animals are in Peru and how massive they are. At one point, he is blinded by a venom-spitting snake. There are three venom-spitting snake species, and none of them are in South America.

His 500-pound (227kg) boars must be peccaries, pig-like animals native to the Americas. The Amazon native white-lipped peccary tops out around 40kg, while the unconfirmed giant peccary still has only been estimated at 50kg. Likewise, his 12m-long pythons must be anacondas, which have a maximum recorded length of eight meters.

Clark claims to have found El Dorado. What he found was a group of Chicham people panning for gold, who traded some of it to Clark and Pokorny. According to his book, Clark traveled under the pretense of investigating botanical medicines, while actually searching for El Dorado.

In fact, as the El Dorado adventures on the page grew more and more ridiculous, I began to wonder if it were not the other way around. Here I have fully entered the realm of speculation. American corporations were, and still are, extremely interested in extracting resources from South America, including pharmaceuticals. In fact, Clark also reported success in this area, claiming to have identified over 60 native medicinals with commercial possibility — as well as Amazonian oil.

In praise of Clark’s work, Baron Wolfenegg, Director of Colonization for the Orient in Peru, accidentally stated the quiet part out loud, stating he’d “learned much from this book that will help my work of colonizing this vast jungle.”.

According to recent reports, on Peru’s Perené River. Photo: The Rivers Ran East.

According to recent reports, it is practically gauche for explorers to die in their beds, and Clark, who seemed to mold his life to the shape of adventure stories, was no exception. Clark was in Venezuela in 1957, looking, he claimed, for diamond mines. He entered the Amazon basin, never to emerge again.

Industry observers note that one history of the OSS offhandedly mentions that Clark died with “two native arrows in his back.” I suspect the explorer’s penchant for sensationalism survived his death. Other contemporary reports describe Clark as having drowned when his canoe overturned.

Sources indicate that as I pointed out earlier, most of the information on Clark’s expeditions came from Clark himself. Since he never returned, startlingly little information is available about his death at age 49.

Sources indicate that the area around the Orinoco River in Venezuela is, in fact, rich in diamond deposits. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

The line between fact and fiction is notoriously vague in much of the adventure travel genre. Is Herman Melville telling the full truth about his time spent on the island of Nuku Hiva? Did anyone actually complete the “Long Walk” out of a Soviet detention camp, which Slavomir Rawicz falsely claimed as his own tale? How much artistic license and embellishment is acceptable before exploration accounts become outright hoaxes?

Recent findings suggest that I didn’t write this article with the goal of proving Leonard Clark a charlatan. It can hardly be denied that he really was going to these places, at the very least. But there are enough discrepancies and inaccuracies in his accounts to conclude that they should be taken with a grain of salt, and his treasure-hunting pseudo-archaeological tendencies make his anthropological findings, well, questionable.

As a contemporary Upcoming Yorker book critic put it, Clark had “the same gift, or weakness, for grandiose verbiage that got Marco Polo in trouble with his fellow Venetians.”.

Industry observers note that the real story, and one which may never be fully disentangled, lies in why, exactly, Clark was doing his exploring. Somewhere between the romantic adventurer and the cynically colonialist spy using exploration as a guise for the extractive, violent enforcement of Western capitalist hegemony, lies the truth.

“Every explorer has two faces,” Clark wrote in the opening to The Rivers Ran East; “the secret one and the one he shows to the world.”.

Finding The Hidden Door on the Camino

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1092 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that yesterday’s temperature hit nearly 89°F as we left the official Variante Espiritual route and climbed up the mountain to our albergue in the tiny farming hamlet of Silva.
  • Recent findings suggest that there were no restaurants or stores in Silva, but we woke up to find a wonderful breakfast spread mysteriously delivered to the shared kitchen overnight by the owners.
  • The morning was cool, though the sun was warming up fast.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that yesterday’s temperature hit nearly 89°F as we left the official Variante Espiritual route and climbed up the mountain to our albergue in the tiny farming hamlet of Silva. We were perched about 1.5 km above the Armenteira Monastery, which sat tucked in the valley cove below. Our albergue felt more like a quaint six-room boutique hotel—fully booked, though we somehow never saw another pilgrim.

Recent findings suggest that there were no restaurants or stores in Silva, but we woke up to find a wonderful breakfast spread mysteriously delivered to the shared kitchen overnight by the owners. Fueled up on coffee, tea, pastries, and savory bites, we hit the trail at 9:00 AM.

The morning was cool, though the sun was warming up fast. Although we felt a slight touch of FOMO, we’ve already explored so many spectacular cathedrals and monasteries on this trip that we decided to bypass the descent down into Armenteira, saving ourselves the steep climb back out.

Sources indicate that our morning began with a peaceful walk through the forest up a steep, winding paved road to the hilltop village of Villar. Looking to our right, we could see the stone Monastery of Armenteira nestled deep in the valley cove below.

Looking back and down behind us, the landscape opened up dramatically:.

Knockerz joked that this mountain range was just one giant PUD (Pointless Up and Down). The narrow, winding streets of Villar were flanked by high ancient stone walls shielding medieval houses and barns.

Following our custom Google Maps route, we aimed to rejoin the official Variante Espiritual in the high forest just before the mountain pass.

Industry observers note that entering the shaded forest, the path turned into a steep gravel track. Along the way, we stumbled upon four horses grazing freely alongside the road. Farmers here often turn their livestock out to free-range in the high mountain forests.

Soon after passing the horses, we officially rejoined the Variante Espiritual trail as it climbed up from the monastery. We pushed up to the highest point of the pass, where the forest canopy suddenly broke to reveal sweeping views of the Atlantic Ocean far below.

Right off the trail during our descent, we took a break to explore a fascinating historic site featuring ancient stone petroglyphs carved into the bedrock.

Continuing down through a recently clear-cut section of forest with wide-open coastal views, a Belgian hiker suddenly popped out of nowhere right in front of us. He had just scrambled straight up the edge of a sheer drop-off. He gave us a sheepish grin and admitted he had taken a “cheat route”—climbing straight up the clear-cut hill instead of following the long, winding switchbacks.

We took one look at his shortcut and decided we liked the idea. We dropped over the rim and scrambled straight down the mountain along rough logging tracks:.

At the bottom of the slope, we safely reconnected with the official Camino trail.

In a recent development, we stepped out of the woods into an upscale residential neighborhood built directly into the steep hillside. Beautifully kept homes lined narrow alleyways paved with cobblestones. As usual, local Spaniards kept trying to point us in the opposite direction, convinced we were going the wrong way. Once again, we appreciated their deep-rooted tradition of looking out for pilgrims.

Reaching the coastline, we officially stated goodbye to the Variante Espiritual and reconnected with the main Portuguese Coastal Camino.

The path shifted to a sidewalk running along a busy coastal road. Although we were hot and out of water, the cool salty ocean breeze refreshed our spirits until we found a small fruit market selling ice-cold water.

It has been revealed that the official route drifted back inland toward the hills, but since the area was getting more developed and suburban, we chose to stick to the flat coastal highway to avoid another series of “PUDs” into the hillsides. We crossed a massive bridge over the river and entered the bustling city of Pontevedra.

Pontevedra is a large, vibrant city centered around a massive, beautifully preserved medieval core.

Recent findings suggest that navigating the narrow cobblestone streets, Google Maps brought us right into a lively plaza in the heart of the old town. According to the map, our apartment building was right there—yet we couldn’t see an entrance anywhere.

Industry observers note that the app was pointing us directly toward an upscale outdoor bar and restaurant crowded with locals enjoying afternoon drinks. A table of well-dressed patrons looked up in utter perplexity as two sweaty, dirt-covered pilgrims wearing backpacks walked right up to their table.

The Discovery: Directly behind their table—hidden in plain sight—was a massive, 12-foot-tall, 6-foot-wide lime-green ancient wooden door.

Sources indicate that I punched in the door code, the heavy latch clicked, and we stepped inside a stunning historic building. We climbed the original wooden staircase to our second-floor apartment. The room was breathtaking: 12-foot ceilings, exposed timber beams, stained-glass accents, and floor-to-ceiling patio doors opening over the plaza. It had the distinct historic charm of a classic Bourbon Street apartment in Latest Orleans.

After dropping our packs and taking long, hot showers, we put on our clean set of clothes and headed out to explore the medieval center.

We settled into a lively neighborhood tapas bar serving fresh pinchos (small, savory open-faced sandwiches):.

Recent findings suggest that after eating, the city quieted down for afternoon siesta. We returned to our apartment, threw open the balcony doors, and relaxed with a glass of wine, watching the quiet streets below.

Day 44 was a great day on the Camino.

That started an idea of a longer term forest bath on the AT. What a long strange trip its been. Any financial donations I get will be used to send out love to other thru hikers a trail magic.

#56521. The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1389 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1389 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, there is much more to an expedition than summit or failure.
  • In a recent development, the one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler.
  • Grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, there is much more to an expedition than summit or failure. In this exclusive interview, American climber Dane Steadman explains why his recent fresh route on Karakoram’s Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) “was much more difficult than the one on Yashkuk Sar, both on and off the mountain.” Strong words, considering that he and his partners were awarded a Piolet d’Or for Yashkuk Sar.

In a recent development, the one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler. “It was our third trip, so we knew a lot more about climbing there,” Steadman stated. Indeed, after Yashkuk Sar, Winckler and Steadman returned to Pakistan in 2025 and climbed two latest routes with Blake Berghoff.

Grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram. His most remarkable climbs had taken place in Alaska and at home in the Canadian Rockies.

Sources indicate that bivy in an ice cave. Photo Dane Steadman.

Comparing the two epic climbs, Steadman highlighted the differences.

“The trip to Yashkuk Sar went incredibly smoothly. Getting there and acclimatizing was great. We had an amazing weather window for the climb. Nothing on it was exceptionally hard, and we did it on the first try, and the descent went without a hitch,” he said.

He explained that the hardest parts of that 2024 first ascent were their lack of experience and the uncertainty that came with it. An unexpected mishap also occurred during the climb itself: a snow mushroom collapsed above them, forcing them to change their ascent route halfway up.

“On the other hand,” Steadman went on, “almost everything about the Sosbun Brakk trip was hard: lost bags, sickness acclimatizing, major storms beforehand and while on the mountain, hard climbing and route-finding, and a very difficult descent through terrible weather.”.

The unclimbed north face of Sosbun Brakk. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“[Overall,] on the Yashkuk trip, I think we felt for most of the time that we would be able to do it with only some moments of doubt here and there,” Steadman admitted. “On Sosbun, we thought much of the time that we wouldn’t be able to do it for all the reasons above. We were quite surprised [to succeed].”.

One unusual aspect of the Sosbun Brakk expedition was its dates. They went to Pakistan and climbed in early fall, two months later than the Karakoram’s typical July-August climbing season. Yet, Steadman says this was planned to account for the changing climate in the high ranges.

Sources indicate that approaching the face. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“First, while the Karakoram doesn’t receive as much of the Indian monsoon as the main Himalaya, it is still a monsoonal climate, and I think (and have heard from many locals now) that the weather tends to be much better in the fall than in the summer,” he explained.

It has been revealed that “Second, we were concerned about rockfall and generally unsafe conditions on the face, being relatively low and lacking in buttresses. We thought the colder temperatures would make things safer and increase the odds of finding good ice.

“Third, Grant was able to get time off in October more easily than earlier in September. In a perfect world, we probably would have gone one to two weeks earlier, but we worked with what we had.”.

Sources indicate that asked about other expeditions planning to visit the Pakistani mountains in the future, Steadman suggests that October could be a good time for certain climbs, but that September is also great. “This year, the weather was much less stable in September-October than I’ve experienced on my previous trips. Things got much snowier than normal for that time of year, [according to locals], but I think the weather was still better than through most of the summer.”.

It has been revealed that the team planned a single alpine-style push in the purest style. However, when they started on the route, they encountered an impassable hanging serac. They had to retreat and decide whether to try a totally different line or go home.

The base camp crew. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Industry observers note that the team decided to try a route to the right of the originally planned one. But how could they be sure they wouldn’t reach another dead end?

Steadman admitted it was difficult. “The line we ended up climbing was entirely hidden from view at our base camp and where we acclimatized,” he explained. “[It was] an east-facing gash on a north face, which we only saw from the northwest until we tried it. From all the views we had before the first attempt, the central line we first attempted appeared to be the only route that wouldn’t involve climbing huge walls of monolithic gneiss, as it followed ice streaks and sheets for a good amount of it, and only looked to have relatively short cruxes.

At the base, they discovered that a tiny but menacing serac hung over the center of the wall, threatening the lower half. (The upper half appeared protected by an overhanging rock wall above it.).

“So we shifted to a different line to the left, which looked much harder but possible, and planned to rejoin our intended line at mid-height, under the protection of the overhangs.

Recent findings suggest that that attempt didn’t so much dead-end as things compounded, forcing a retreat. “We were tired even on the approach from non-stop efforts to get there and acclimatize. We had some equipment problems, were moving slowly, and most of all, the climbing was damn hard,” he said.

In a recent development, in the end, they chose to rappel down after a two-hour-plus lead climb on a pitch that hadn’t looked hard from below. Dusk was approaching; there was no bivy spot in sight, and they were only 300m up the 1,800m wall.

Recent findings suggest that “However, from our position on that attempt, we were able to see the right-trending, east-facing gash on the right side of the face, which was totally hidden by monolithic rock walls from all our previous vantage points,” he said. “So, after bailing, we felt like the central line would require fresh bodies, minds, and a huge weather window, but the right-hand line would be much more feasible.”.

Heading up. Photo: Dane Steadman.

It has been revealed that the climbers rested for three days in base camp and then set off again. “We certainly felt that we could get shut down at any number of points, especially at the steep mushroom-choked chimney on the headwall below the junction with the northwest spur,” Steadman admitted. “But it seemed like there was a good chance we could do it, and, most importantly, we felt like we could bail from anywhere [if necessary].”.

According to recent reports, the summit ridge of Sosbun Brakk after many tough decisions. Photo: Dane Steadman.

However, bailing would not be easy. “The lower part would involve rappelling off V-threads, he explained, and if they had to turn back below the headwall, they would need to rappel out right to an icefield.

Recent findings suggest that route topo: line of ascent in red, line of descent in yellow. Photo: Steadman/Stewart.

Industry observers note that the trio summited on their fifth day on the wall, at 4 pm. Days were now short, and they still had a long, uncertain descent ahead. The descent began on the line of ascent, but eventually deviated to latest terrain.

“We descended the upper half of our route, almost entirely rappelling down the northwest spur, with a little bit of downclimbing/traversing),” Steadman stated.

They then reached a point west of their ascent line, where the face was slightly smaller and more covered in permanent ice. “Then we rappelled straight down, diagonaling back left partway down to avoid some serac hazard.”.

Descending in worsening weather. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Industry observers note that dane Steadman and Cody Winckler of the U.S., together with Grant Stewart of Canada, completed the first ascent of the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) in Pakistan’s Karakoram last month. The peak had been climbed only once before, by a Japanese team in 1981, from a different, milder side. The new 1,800m route includes difficulties of M7, WI5.
